record.title: Data from eLocust3m, cleaned by AI, supports FAO's control of locusts in East Africa, which may have averted USD 1.56 billion in losses
record.summary: PlantVillage's eLocust3m app gathered over 240,000 locust records. AI removed unusable ones for the control operation that FAO credits with averting USD 1.56 billion in losses.
record.account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings. Algorithms checked the photos. Penn State extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. The wider operation used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. On 8 April 2021 The New York Times reported that PlantVillage scouts had collected over 240,000 records in a year. Government personnel contributed alongside citizens. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand, who said that swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel. In a feature of 6 May 2021, FAO says that it received up to 2,500 records a day. It says that nearly 25 percent were unusable or incorrect. FAO asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to find the unwanted data. PlantVillage was to remove it before FAO shared locations with control teams on the ground. Teams in the air got the locations. FAO says that East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal. It says that they prevented the loss of 800 million liters of milk. It says that they protected the food security of 36.6 million people and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses. On 15 June 2022 FAO declared the East Africa upsurge over. It said that it had trained 3,800 people across the region to use applications such as eLocust3 to report locusts. In May 2026 Serdo and Nemeth, who have no tie to FAO or PlantVillage, published a review in Frontiers in Zoology. They named eLocust3m among the tools of the response in 2020 and 2021. They restate FAO's figures without new analysis.
record.purpose: PlantVillage built the app with FAO so that anyone with a smartphone can record georeferenced locust sightings. Its AI checks photos and removes unusable records, so that FAO can direct survey and control teams.

fields.account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings. Algorithms checked the photos. Penn State extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. The wider operation used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. On 8 April 2021 The New York Times reported that PlantVillage scouts had collected over 240,000 records in a year. Government personnel contributed alongside citizens. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand, who said that swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel. In a feature of 6 May 2021, FAO says that it received up to 2,500 records a day. It says that nearly 25 percent were unusable or incorrect. FAO asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to find the unwanted data. PlantVillage was to remove it before FAO shared locations with control teams on the ground. Teams in the air got the locations. FAO says that East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal. It says that they prevented the loss of 800 million liters of milk. It says that they protected the food security of 36.6 million people and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses. On 15 June 2022 FAO declared the East Africa upsurge over. It said that it had trained 3,800 people across the region to use applications such as eLocust3 to report locusts. In May 2026 Serdo and Nemeth, who have no tie to FAO or PlantVillage, published a review in Frontiers in Zoology. They named eLocust3m among the tools of the response in 2020 and 2021. They restate FAO's figures without new analysis.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The decisions do not compare enforcement with and without the alerts, and no court tested their accuracy. IAT analysts set each alert against other satellite images, and some cases add overflights or site visits. MapBiomas states that analysts validate each alert on Planet images and that a supervised Random Forest classifier refines its outline. In the lead case the court treats the tools as artificial intelligence and finds that a human was in the loop, but it does not describe the models.

record.title: Paraná's Court of Justice upheld IAT enforcement against Atlantic Forest clearing flagged by MapBiomas Alerta in nine decisions from 2024 to 2026
record.summary: Paraná's Court of Justice upheld IAT enforcement in nine decisions from 2024 to 2026 on Atlantic Forest clearing flagged by MapBiomas alerts. None rejected the satellite evidence.
record.account: MapBiomas compiles deforestation alerts. It has analysts validate each on Planet images. It refines each alert's outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Paraná's environmental agency is the Instituto Água e Terra (IAT). Its analysts check such alerts in the satellite reports behind its infraction notices, sometimes without a site visit. From November 2024 to September 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided nine cases built on these notices. It upheld or imposed fines, embargoes and repair orders in four civil appeals. Three interim rulings treated the notices as presumed true, though one suspended R$104,000 in fines as disproportionate for a small farmer. By majority, the court let a prosecution over 116.2 ha go ahead. It upheld a conviction. In the lead case, it found that human operators had compared before-and-after images on MapBiomas, Google Earth Pro and the federal Brasil MAIS platform. It called the agency's conclusions "epistemologicamente confiáveis", epistemologically reliable. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. In both criminal cases, a dissenting judge held that the reports could not replace a forensic exam. No court measured the alerts' accuracy.
record.purpose: MapBiomas built MapBiomas Alerta to compile, validate and refine deforestation alerts from detection systems across Brazil and to publish each confirmed clearing with a report.
record.system: MapBiomas Alerta, checked in IAT reports with alerts of the federal Brasil MAIS satellite platform (the decisions call it 'Mapbiomas', 'Mapa Biomas' or 'Alerta Mapbiomas')
record.developer: MapBiomas (MapBiomas Alerta), which compiles source alerts from other detection systems. The lead case also names the SCCON web platform of the Programa Brasil Mais, a system of the Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública.
record.deployer: Instituto Água e Terra (IAT), Paraná's environmental agency, through its geographic intelligence unit (NGI) and inspectors. The Ministério Público do Paraná brought the civil actions and prosecutions.
record.location: Paraná, Brazil (cases from Irati, Rebouças, Dois Vizinhos, Guarapuava, Telêmaco Borba, Cantagalo, Marmeleiro and Bocaiúva do Sul)

fields.account: MapBiomas compiles deforestation alerts. It has analysts validate each on Planet images. It refines each alert's outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Paraná's environmental agency is the Instituto Água e Terra (IAT). Its analysts check such alerts in the satellite reports behind its infraction notices, sometimes without a site visit. From November 2024 to September 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided nine cases built on these notices. It upheld or imposed fines, embargoes and repair orders in four civil appeals. Three interim rulings treated the notices as presumed true, though one suspended R$104,000 in fines as disproportionate for a small farmer. By majority, the court let a prosecution over 116.2 ha go ahead. It upheld a conviction. In the lead case, it found that human operators had compared before-and-after images on MapBiomas, Google Earth Pro and the federal Brasil MAIS platform. It called the agency's conclusions "epistemologicamente confiáveis", epistemologically reliable. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. In both criminal cases, a dissenting judge held that the reports could not replace a forensic exam. No court measured the alerts' accuracy.

fields.account: MapBiomas compiles deforestation alerts. It has analysts validate each on Planet images. It refines each alert's outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Paraná's environmental agency is the Instituto Água e Terra (IAT). Its analysts check such alerts in the satellite reports behind its infraction notices, sometimes without a site visit. From November 2024 to September 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided nine cases built on these notices. It upheld or imposed fines, embargoes and repair orders in four civil appeals. Three interim rulings treated the notices as presumed true, though one suspended R$104,000 in fines as disproportionate for a small farmer. By majority, the court let a prosecution over 116.2 ha go ahead. It upheld a conviction. In the lead case, it found that human operators had compared before-and-after images on MapBiomas, Google Earth Pro and the federal Brasil MAIS platform. It called the agency's conclusions "epistemologicamente confiáveis", epistemologically reliable. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. In both criminal cases, a dissenting judge held that the reports could not replace a forensic exam. No court measured the alerts' accuracy.

fields.headline: Paraná court upholds nine IAT forest cases built on *MapBiomas Alerta*

fields.account: MapBiomas compiles deforestation alerts. It has analysts validate each on Planet images. It refines each alert's outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Paraná's environmental agency is the Instituto Água e Terra (IAT). Its analysts check such alerts in the satellite reports behind its infraction notices, sometimes without a site visit. From November 2024 to September 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided nine cases built on these notices. It upheld or imposed fines, embargoes and repair orders in four civil appeals. Three interim rulings treated the notices as presumed true, though one suspended R$104,000 in fines as disproportionate for a small farmer. By majority, the court let a prosecution over 116.2 ha go ahead. It upheld a conviction. In the lead case, it found that human operators had compared before-and-after images on MapBiomas, Google Earth Pro and the federal Brasil MAIS platform. It called the agency's conclusions "epistemologicamente confiáveis", epistemologically reliable. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. In both criminal cases, a dissenting judge held that the reports could not replace a forensic exam. No court measured the alerts' accuracy.

produced_by: MapBiomas validated each alert on high-resolution images and published a report for it.
IAT analysts compared satellite images from before and after each clearing and checked alerts from MapBiomas and the Brasil MAIS network.
The IAT issued infraction notices and embargoes from those reports, in some cases without a site visit.
State prosecutors brought civil actions and prosecutions on the notices.
must_hold: A human operator must compare images from before and after the clearing before a notice is issued.
Each notice must give coordinates, images and the vegetation's stage of regeneration so that the person fined can contest it.
Courts must presume the notices true until the person fined proves otherwise.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The decisions do not describe how the alerts are made, and none compares enforcement with and without them. MapBiomas's method page says that it compiles alerts from other detection systems, including SAD Mata Atlântica of SOS Mata Atlântica and ArcPlan. It says that trained analysts check each alert visually on Planet and Sentinel-2 images. It adds that a supervised Random Forest classifier in Google Earth Engine then refines the outline of each confirmed clearing. That refinement is the machine-learning step that MapBiomas documents. One officer named SOS Mata Atlântica as the source of an alert. The decisions do not show which version of the method applied to alerts from 2019 to 2023. Where the decisions describe the inspections, officers checked each alert on site before they acted.

record.title: Santa Catarina's Court of Justice upheld police enforcement in 15 decisions on Atlantic Forest clearing first flagged by MapBiomas Alerta
record.summary: Santa Catarina's Court of Justice upheld police enforcement in 15 decisions from 2023 to 2025 on Atlantic Forest clearing that MapBiomas alerts had flagged. None rejected the satellite evidence.
record.account: From August 2023 to September 2025, Santa Catarina's Court of Justice decided 15 appeals in cases begun by MapBiomas Alerta deforestation alerts. The state's military environmental police received the alerts, mostly in the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé. Officers inspected the alerts on site. They found clearings of 0.99 to 11.05 hectares of Atlantic Forest. In 13 criminal appeals, the court upheld 11 convictions. It convicted two defendants whom trial judges had acquitted. It reduced two of the upheld penalties. In two civil cases, it upheld a restoration order with R$37,000 in collective moral damages. It refused to annul infraction notices. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. One officer testified that the damage flagged by a MapBiomas alert was confirmed on site. In another case, the court dated the clearing from the images behind an alert. It called them “dotados de precisão técnica”, technically precise. MapBiomas says that analysts validate each alert. It says that they refine its outline with a Random Forest classifier, which the court did not examine. Officers reported flaws in alerts: a missed cleared area, an understated one and the inclusion of older clearing.
record.purpose: MapBiomas built MapBiomas Alerta to compile, validate and refine deforestation alerts from detection systems across Brazil and to publish each confirmed clearing with a report.
record.system: MapBiomas Alerta (the decisions call it 'MapBiomas', 'Mapa Biomas' or 'MapBiomas Alerta')
record.developer: MapBiomas (MapBiomas Alerta), which compiles source alerts from other detection systems
record.deployer: Polícia Militar Ambiental de Santa Catarina (Santa Catarina's military environmental police), mostly in the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé with the Ministério Público de Santa Catarina
record.location: Santa Catarina, Brazil (rural properties in Canoinhas, Mafra, Rio Negrinho, Santa Cecília, Lebon Régis and other municipalities)

ratings.reason: Alerts led police patrols to cleared areas of 0.99 to 11.05 hectares, and the court decided for the enforcement in all 15 appeals.
The decisions record convictions, a restoration order and infraction notices, but none reports whether forest grew back or whether clearing fell.

produced_by: MapBiomas Alerta published deforestation alerts with polygons over rural properties in Santa Catarina.
The military environmental police received the alerts, mostly during the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé with the Ministério Público de Santa Catarina.
Officers inspected the alerts on site, mapped the clearings with drones and compared older satellite images to date them.
The police issued infraction notices and embargoes, and prosecutors brought criminal charges or civil actions.
must_hold: Officers must check each alert on the ground, because some alerts missed, understated or overstated a clearing.
The police must link each alert polygon to the person responsible for the land.
Courts must accept police inspection reports, drone surveys and satellite images without a formal forensic examination.

ai_role.statement: The decisions do not describe how the alerts are made, and none compares enforcement with and without them. MapBiomas's method page says that it compiles alerts from other detection systems, including SAD Mata Atlântica of SOS Mata Atlântica and ArcPlan. It says that trained analysts check each alert visually on Planet and Sentinel-2 images. It adds that a supervised Random Forest classifier in Google Earth Engine then refines the outline of each confirmed clearing. That refinement is the machine-learning step that MapBiomas documents. One officer named SOS Mata Atlântica as the source of an alert. The decisions do not show which version of the method applied to alerts from 2019 to 2023. Where the decisions describe the inspections, officers checked each alert on site before they acted.

fields.account: From August 2023 to September 2025, Santa Catarina's Court of Justice decided 15 appeals in cases begun by MapBiomas Alerta deforestation alerts. The state's military environmental police received the alerts, mostly in the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé. Officers inspected the alerts on site. They found clearings of 0.99 to 11.05 hectares of Atlantic Forest. In 13 criminal appeals, the court upheld 11 convictions. It convicted two defendants whom trial judges had acquitted. It reduced two of the upheld penalties. In two civil cases, it upheld a restoration order with R$37,000 in collective moral damages. It refused to annul infraction notices. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. One officer testified that the damage flagged by a MapBiomas alert was confirmed on site. In another case, the court dated the clearing from the images behind an alert. It called them “dotados de precisão técnica”, technically precise. MapBiomas says that analysts validate each alert. It says that they refine its outline with a Random Forest classifier, which the court did not examine. Officers reported flaws in alerts: a missed cleared area, an understated one and the inclusion of older clearing.

fields.summary: Santa Catarina's Court of Justice upheld police enforcement in 15 decisions from 2023 to 2025 on Atlantic Forest clearing that MapBiomas alerts had flagged. None rejected the satellite evidence.
fields.account: From August 2023 to September 2025, Santa Catarina's Court of Justice decided 15 appeals in cases begun by MapBiomas Alerta deforestation alerts. The state's military environmental police received the alerts, mostly in the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé. Officers inspected the alerts on site. They found clearings of 0.99 to 11.05 hectares of Atlantic Forest. In 13 criminal appeals, the court upheld 11 convictions. It convicted two defendants whom trial judges had acquitted. It reduced two of the upheld penalties. In two civil cases, it upheld a restoration order with R$37,000 in collective moral damages. It refused to annul infraction notices. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. One officer testified that the damage flagged by a MapBiomas alert was confirmed on site. In another case, the court dated the clearing from the images behind an alert. It called them “dotados de precisão técnica”, technically precise. MapBiomas says that analysts validate each alert. It says that they refine its outline with a Random Forest classifier, which the court did not examine. Officers reported flaws in alerts: a missed cleared area, an understated one and the inclusion of older clearing.

fields.headline: Santa Catarina court upholds 15 forest cases begun by *MapBiomas Alerta*

fields.account: From August 2023 to September 2025, Santa Catarina's Court of Justice decided 15 appeals in cases begun by MapBiomas Alerta deforestation alerts. The state's military environmental police received the alerts, mostly in the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé. Officers inspected the alerts on site. They found clearings of 0.99 to 11.05 hectares of Atlantic Forest. In 13 criminal appeals, the court upheld 11 convictions. It convicted two defendants whom trial judges had acquitted. It reduced two of the upheld penalties. In two civil cases, it upheld a restoration order with R$37,000 in collective moral damages. It refused to annul infraction notices. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. One officer testified that the damage flagged by a MapBiomas alert was confirmed on site. In another case, the court dated the clearing from the images behind an alert. It called them “dotados de precisão técnica”, technically precise. MapBiomas says that analysts validate each alert. It says that they refine its outline with a Random Forest classifier, which the court did not examine. Officers reported flaws in alerts: a missed cleared area, an understated one and the inclusion of older clearing.

produced_by: MapBiomas Alerta published deforestation alerts with polygons over rural properties in Santa Catarina.
The military environmental police received the alerts, mostly during the yearly Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé with the Ministério Público de Santa Catarina.
Officers inspected the alerts on site, mapped the clearings with drones and compared older satellite images to date them.
The police issued infraction notices and embargoes, and prosecutors brought criminal charges or civil actions.
must_hold: Officers must check each alert on the ground, because some alerts missed, understated or overstated a clearing.
The police must link each alert polygon to the person responsible for the land.
Courts must accept police inspection reports, drone surveys and satellite images without a formal forensic examination.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The decisions do not describe how the alerts are made, and none compares enforcement with and without them. Officers checked each alert by satellite comparison, drone or site visit before they acted, and no court tested the alerts' accuracy. MapBiomas states that analysts validate each alert on Planet images and that a supervised Random Forest classifier refines its outline.

record.title: Paraná's Court of Justice upheld police enforcement against Atlantic Forest clearing flagged by MapBiomas Alerta in 10 decisions from 2023 to 2026
record.summary: Paraná's Court of Justice upheld police enforcement in 10 decisions from 2023 to 2026 on Atlantic Forest clearing flagged by MapBiomas alerts, three by reversing acquittals.
record.account: Paraná's military environmental police, the Batalhão de Polícia Ambiental Força Verde, receive MapBiomas deforestation alerts as complaints. Many arrive during Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé, a task force that state prosecutors coordinate. MapBiomas has analysts validate each alert. It refines the outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Teams check each alert by satellite comparison, drone or site visit. From June 2023 to August 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided 10 cases that involved such checks. In six criminal appeals it upheld or imposed convictions, three by reversing acquittals, one of them for three of five defendants, each over a dissent that called for a forensic exam. In four civil cases it upheld repair orders or kept notices in force. It struck collective damages in one. In another it suspended an order to file a recovery plan. Officers testified that the cleared area in the field often exceeds the alert. They testified that flagged vegetation is sometimes not native. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. No court measured the alerts' accuracy. A further conviction, from a 2018 inspection that predates MapBiomas's alerts, is kept as context.
record.purpose: MapBiomas built MapBiomas Alerta to compile, validate and refine deforestation alerts from detection systems across Brazil and to publish each confirmed clearing with a report.
record.system: MapBiomas Alerta (the decisions call it 'MapBiomas', 'Mapa Biomas', 'MAP BIOMAS' or 'Alerta Biomas')
record.developer: MapBiomas (MapBiomas Alerta), which compiles source alerts from other detection systems
record.deployer: Polícia Militar Ambiental do Paraná (Batalhão de Polícia Ambiental Força Verde), Paraná's military environmental police, often in Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé with the Ministério Público do Paraná, which brought the cases
record.location: Paraná, Brazil (cases from Ortigueira, Londrina, Altônia, Prudentópolis, Rio Negro, Guarapuava, Laranjeiras do Sul, Piraí do Sul and Castro)

ratings.reason: Alerts led police teams to cleared areas, and the court upheld or imposed convictions in six appeals and upheld repair orders or notices in four civil cases.
The decisions record convictions, repair orders and notices, but none reports whether the forest grew back or whether clearing fell.

ai_role.statement: The decisions do not describe how the alerts are made, and none compares enforcement with and without them. Officers checked each alert by satellite comparison, drone or site visit before they acted, and no court tested the alerts' accuracy. MapBiomas states that analysts validate each alert on Planet images and that a supervised Random Forest classifier refines its outline.

fields.account: Paraná's military environmental police, the Batalhão de Polícia Ambiental Força Verde, receive MapBiomas deforestation alerts as complaints. Many arrive during Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé, a task force that state prosecutors coordinate. MapBiomas has analysts validate each alert. It refines the outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Teams check each alert by satellite comparison, drone or site visit. From June 2023 to August 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided 10 cases that involved such checks. In six criminal appeals it upheld or imposed convictions, three by reversing acquittals, one of them for three of five defendants, each over a dissent that called for a forensic exam. In four civil cases it upheld repair orders or kept notices in force. It struck collective damages in one. In another it suspended an order to file a recovery plan. Officers testified that the cleared area in the field often exceeds the alert. They testified that flagged vegetation is sometimes not native. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. No court measured the alerts' accuracy. A further conviction, from a 2018 inspection that predates MapBiomas's alerts, is kept as context.

fields.summary: Paraná's Court of Justice upheld police enforcement in 10 decisions from 2023 to 2026 on Atlantic Forest clearing flagged by MapBiomas alerts, three by reversing acquittals.
fields.account: Paraná's military environmental police, the Batalhão de Polícia Ambiental Força Verde, receive MapBiomas deforestation alerts as complaints. Many arrive during Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé, a task force that state prosecutors coordinate. MapBiomas has analysts validate each alert. It refines the outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. Teams check each alert by satellite comparison, drone or site visit. From June 2023 to August 2026, the Court of Justice of Paraná decided 10 cases that involved such checks. In six criminal appeals it upheld or imposed convictions, three by reversing acquittals, one of them for three of five defendants, each over a dissent that called for a forensic exam. In four civil cases it upheld repair orders or kept notices in force. It struck collective damages in one. In another it suspended an order to file a recovery plan. Officers testified that the cleared area in the field often exceeds the alert. They testified that flagged vegetation is sometimes not native. No decision rejected the satellite evidence. No court measured the alerts' accuracy. A further conviction, from a 2018 inspection that predates MapBiomas's alerts, is kept as context.

produced_by: MapBiomas alerts reached the police as complaints, often during Operação Mata Atlântica em Pé with state prosecutors.
Teams checked each alert by satellite comparison, drone overflight or a site visit and measured the area with GPS.
The police filed infraction notices, police reports and georeferencing records, and prosecutors brought charges or civil actions.
must_hold: Officers must confirm each alert in the field or by overflight, since field areas often differ from the alert.
The police must identify the person responsible for the land.
Courts must accept police records and testimony when no forensic exam was made.

record.title: CBP facial comparison at Dulles flags a French-passport impostor with a Congolese ID in his shoe on day three
record.summary: On 22 August 2018 CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles flagged a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport. Officers found a Congolese ID in his shoe. He was returned to Brazil.
record.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. In a release, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) states that the officer used the facial comparison technology. It confirmed that the man did not match the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News that the man was apprehended. He said that officers processed him. He said that they returned him to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. The vendor of the matching algorithm has not been named. In a September 2020 audit, the U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that CBP officials said that air entry facial recognition had helped identify seven impostors by December 2019. Gizmodo reported on 11 February 2021 that, in its annual report for fiscal year 2020, CBP showed no impostor flagged at any airport that year. CBP had scanned over 23 million travelers at entry, exit and Preclearance points. Gizmodo also reported that CBP facial recognition detected fewer than 100 impostors at pedestrian crossings that year. In a release of 24 September 2021, CBP reports that facial biometrics had stopped, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally since September 2018.
record.purpose: U.S. Customs and Border Protection uses the system to check arriving travelers against passport or visa photos that the government holds, to catch impostors and speed entry.

ratings.reason: An attempt to enter the United States on a French passport that was not his was stopped and the traveler removed. No further threat beyond the document fraud is documented.

data.retained_case_account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. CBP's release states the officer used the facial comparison biometric technology, which confirmed the man was not a match to the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News the man was apprehended, processed and returned to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. CBP releases record a second (8 September 2018) and third (1 October 2018) impostor at Dulles and, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally. The sources do not name the matching-algorithm vendor.

fields.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. In a release, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) states that the officer used the facial comparison technology. It confirmed that the man did not match the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News that the man was apprehended. He said that officers processed him. He said that they returned him to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. The vendor of the matching algorithm has not been named. In a September 2020 audit, the U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that CBP officials said that air entry facial recognition had helped identify seven impostors by December 2019. Gizmodo reported on 11 February 2021 that, in its annual report for fiscal year 2020, CBP showed no impostor flagged at any airport that year. CBP had scanned over 23 million travelers at entry, exit and Preclearance points. Gizmodo also reported that CBP facial recognition detected fewer than 100 impostors at pedestrian crossings that year. In a release of 24 September 2021, CBP reports that facial biometrics had stopped, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally since September 2018.

record.title: UNDP's evaluation office finds that Libya's election commission uses eMonitor+ to respond to violent content against women politicians
record.summary: UNDP's evaluation office found that Libya's election commission now uses eMonitor+ to respond with targeted communications. The tool finds violent content directed at women politicians.
record.account: UNDP's Regional Bureau for Arab States developed eMonitor+ to scan online media for electoral violations. It scans for hate speech. Online violence against women is one of its targets. In a release of 9 August 2022, UNDP states that eMonitor+ uses machine learning. In August 2022 Libya's High National Elections Commission (HNEC) trained media monitors to use it, with support from UNDP and the UN Support Mission in Libya. The commission's Women Support Unit, set up with UNDP support in 2022, launched the platform to combat online violence against women candidates. In December 2025, UNDP's Independent Evaluation Office published its evaluation of UNDP's work in Libya. The team visited Libya in November 2024. It held over 150 interviews. The office found that HNEC now uses eMonitor+, which employs artificial intelligence to flag violent content directed at women politicians. This lets the commission respond with targeted communications. In November 2023 the same office reported that eMonitor+ data in Libya supported the commission's strategies for reaching women. The 2025 evaluators give no count of flagged posts. They do not count responses. They found that disinformation remains a challenge. Their findings show that hate speech is a continuing challenge.

record.title: Apple Watch Fall Detection summoning help after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
record.summary: As a 69-year-old runner collapsed in cardiac arrest, Fall Detection on an Apple Watch Series 10 called emergency services. It alerted his emergency contacts. He made a full neurological recovery.
record.account: In a case report published on 12 August 2026, the authors describe a 69-year-old man who collapsed from ventricular fibrillation while running alone. He was on a dead-end road, hidden behind a hedge. The paper gives no date. It gives no place. The authors' hospitals are Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen and Slingeland Hospital in Doetinchem. His Apple Watch (reported as Apple Watch 10) with Fall Detection enabled detected the fall. It automatically alerted the emergency medical services by calling 112. It alerted his predefined emergency contacts. Family members who reached him found him unresponsive. They began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance arrived about 1.5 minutes later. Its crew defibrillated him. They restored circulation. He underwent coronary artery bypass grafting. He received an implanted defibrillator. He was discharged on day 29. He made a full neurological recovery. In two earlier interviews, the patient is a 69-year-old man from Varsseveld. The interviews give 1 January 2026 as the date of the collapse. Men's Health NL (28 April 2026) opens “1 januari 2026 begint voor de 69-jarige [name withheld] als een gewone hardloopdag. De fanatieke loper uit Varsseveld is in training voor de halve marathon van Montferland” (1 January 2026 begins for 69-year-old [name withheld] as an ordinary running day. The keen runner from Varsseveld is training for the Montferland half marathon). His son says “De locatie was heel precies. Hij lag achter een heg op een afgelegen plek. Zonder die melding had ik hem niet zo snel gevonden” (the location was very precise. He was lying behind a hedge in a remote spot. Without that alert I would not have found him so quickly). WANT (1 May 2026) quotes him, “Ik weet via mijn activiteitenlog dat ik om twaalf over twaalf aan mijn trainingsrondje begon” (I know from my activity log that I started my training loop at twelve past twelve). It reproduces the alert that his son received, headed “do 1 jan, 12:12”. The interviews match the paper on the man's age, his Apple Watch Series 10 with fall detection, its automatic alert to 112, its alert to his emergency contacts, the hedge, the remote spot, the son starting resuscitation and the daughter giving mouth-to-mouth. They match on a history of asthma, bronchiectasis, six days in intensive care, four bypass grafts, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and a full recovery. No source links the runner to the paper, so the identification is inferred from these details. Men's Health says that the runner also pressed the SOS button himself. It says that a pulse returned within about three minutes. The paper's timeline does not support that. Resuscitation began after 6–7 minutes, according to the paper. Circulation returned after four shocks, adrenaline and amiodarone. The street is probable but inferred. A pager message to the fire brigade on 1 January 2026 at 12:18:59 records a resuscitation on the Oude Doetinchemseweg in Varsseveld. The map in the screenshot of the alert shows the pin on a side road off the Doetinchemseweg. No source links the street to the runner. WANT reported on 1 May 2026 that the runner had spent two months in rehabilitation. It reported that he planned to run the Doetinchem half marathon in October 2026. He had written to Apple's chief executive, Tim Cook, to thank him. He received a reply.
record.purpose: Fall Detection is built to recognize a hard fall and, if the wearer stays immobile, to call emergency services and notify contacts with the location. That is what it did.
record.system: Apple Watch Fall Detection

ratings.reason: The man was alone and hidden from view in cardiac arrest. The automatic alerts brought family members, who began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. He left hospital neurologically intact, and the authors present the outcome as life-saving.

ai_role.statement: The authors report that the watch recognized the fall, called 112 on its own and alerted emergency contacts. Those alerts brought responders to the man behind the hedge. Humans provided resuscitation, defibrillation, and surgery. The watch's contribution is documented in the clinical narrative, but the time to rescue or outcome without it cannot be measured from this case. Apple describes the steps of detection and notification without disclosing the classifier or the version of the model.

record.brief: A case report in Resuscitation Plus, published on 12 August 2026, concerns a 69-year-old man who collapsed in ventricular fibrillation while running alone. He was hidden behind a hedge on a dead-end road.[1] On detecting the fall, his Apple Watch automatically called emergency services on 112 and alerted his emergency contacts. Family members began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance crew arrived about 1.5 minutes later and defibrillated him. He made a full neurological recovery. It is a single documented case, and a similar one appeared in an earlier German report. The authors document that the alerts brought his family to him. They cannot show how long he would have lain there without the alerts. That comparison rests on an interview in which a son says that he would not otherwise have found his father so quickly.[2]

data.retained_case_account: A case report published on 12 August 2026 describes a 69-year-old man who collapsed from ventricular fibrillation while running alone. He was on a dead-end road, hidden behind a hedge. The paper gives no date or place. The authors' hospitals are Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, and Slingeland Hospital, Doetinchem. His Apple Watch (reported as Apple Watch 10) with Fall Detection enabled detected the fall. It automatically alerted his predefined emergency contacts and the emergency medical services by calling 112. Family members reached him, found him unresponsive and began cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance arrived about 1.5 minutes later, defibrillated him and restored circulation. He underwent coronary artery bypass grafting and defibrillator implantation, was discharged on day 29 and made a full neurological recovery. Two interviews identify the patient as a 69-year-old man from Varsseveld, and date the collapse to 1 January 2026. Men's Health NL (28 April 2026) opens “1 januari 2026 begint voor de 69-jarige [name withheld] als een gewone hardloopdag. De fanatieke loper uit Varsseveld is in training voor de halve marathon van Montferland” (1 January 2026 begins for 69-year-old [name withheld] as an ordinary running day; the keen runner from Varsseveld is training for the Montferland half marathon). His son says “De locatie was heel precies. Hij lag achter een heg op een afgelegen plek. Zonder die melding had ik hem niet zo snel gevonden” (the location was very precise; he was lying behind a hedge in a remote spot; without that alert I would not have found him so quickly). WANT (1 May 2026) quotes him, “Ik weet via mijn activiteitenlog dat ik om twaalf over twaalf aan mijn trainingsrondje begon” (I know from my activity log that I started my training loop at twelve past twelve). It reproduces the alert his son received, headed “do 1 jan, 12:12”. The interviews match the paper on the man's age and the Apple Watch Series 10 with fall detection. They also match on the automatic alert to 112 and to his emergency contacts, the hedge and the remote spot. They match on the son starting CPR and the daughter giving mouth-to-mouth, and a history of asthma and bronchiectasis. They match on six days in intensive care, four bypass grafts, an ICD and a full recovery. No source names both the paper and the runner, so the identification is inferred from these details. Men's Health says that the runner also pressed the SOS button himself and that a pulse returned within about three minutes. The paper's timeline does not support that: CPR after 6–7 minutes, four shocks, adrenaline and amiodarone before circulation returned. The street is probable but inferred. A fire-brigade pager message of 1 January 2026 at 12:18:59 records a resuscitation on the Oude Doetinchemseweg in Varsseveld. That is a dead-end road at the western edge of the village. The map in the alert screenshot shows the pin on a side road off the Doetinchemseweg. No source names the street in connection with the runner.

fields.summary: As a 69-year-old runner collapsed in cardiac arrest, Fall Detection on an Apple Watch Series 10 called emergency services. It alerted his emergency contacts. He made a full neurological recovery.
fields.account: In a case report published on 12 August 2026, the authors describe a 69-year-old man who collapsed from ventricular fibrillation while running alone. He was on a dead-end road, hidden behind a hedge. The paper gives no date. It gives no place. The authors' hospitals are Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen and Slingeland Hospital in Doetinchem. His Apple Watch (reported as Apple Watch 10) with Fall Detection enabled detected the fall. It automatically alerted the emergency medical services by calling 112. It alerted his predefined emergency contacts. Family members who reached him found him unresponsive. They began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance arrived about 1.5 minutes later. Its crew defibrillated him. They restored circulation. He underwent coronary artery bypass grafting. He received an implanted defibrillator. He was discharged on day 29. He made a full neurological recovery. In two earlier interviews, the patient is a 69-year-old man from Varsseveld. The interviews give 1 January 2026 as the date of the collapse. Men's Health NL (28 April 2026) opens “1 januari 2026 begint voor de 69-jarige [name withheld] als een gewone hardloopdag. De fanatieke loper uit Varsseveld is in training voor de halve marathon van Montferland” (1 January 2026 begins for 69-year-old [name withheld] as an ordinary running day. The keen runner from Varsseveld is training for the Montferland half marathon). His son says “De locatie was heel precies. Hij lag achter een heg op een afgelegen plek. Zonder die melding had ik hem niet zo snel gevonden” (the location was very precise. He was lying behind a hedge in a remote spot. Without that alert I would not have found him so quickly). WANT (1 May 2026) quotes him, “Ik weet via mijn activiteitenlog dat ik om twaalf over twaalf aan mijn trainingsrondje begon” (I know from my activity log that I started my training loop at twelve past twelve). It reproduces the alert that his son received, headed “do 1 jan, 12:12”. The interviews match the paper on the man's age, his Apple Watch Series 10 with fall detection, its automatic alert to 112, its alert to his emergency contacts, the hedge, the remote spot, the son starting resuscitation and the daughter giving mouth-to-mouth. They match on a history of asthma, bronchiectasis, six days in intensive care, four bypass grafts, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and a full recovery. No source links the runner to the paper, so the identification is inferred from these details. Men's Health says that the runner also pressed the SOS button himself. It says that a pulse returned within about three minutes. The paper's timeline does not support that. Resuscitation began after 6–7 minutes, according to the paper. Circulation returned after four shocks, adrenaline and amiodarone. The street is probable but inferred. A pager message to the fire brigade on 1 January 2026 at 12:18:59 records a resuscitation on the Oude Doetinchemseweg in Varsseveld. The map in the screenshot of the alert shows the pin on a side road off the Doetinchemseweg. No source links the street to the runner. WANT reported on 1 May 2026 that the runner had spent two months in rehabilitation. It reported that he planned to run the Doetinchem half marathon in October 2026. He had written to Apple's chief executive, Tim Cook, to thank him. He received a reply.

record.title: A CIA tool called “Ghost Murmur”, pairing quantum magnetometry with AI, may have located downed F-15E officer “Dude 44 Bravo” in Iran before his rescue in April 2026, but CBS later reports that unnamed CIA technology pinpointed him
record.summary: Two anonymous sources credit the CIA's Ghost Murmur, quantum sensing paired with AI, with locating a downed F-15E officer in Iran. CBS reports that CIA technology pinpointed him. It names no tool.
record.account: The White House briefing of 6 April 2026 documents the rescue of the downed F-15E weapons systems officer in Iran. In the official transcript, the speakers describe watching his suspected position with a camera from 40 miles away. That distance concerns the camera. No source establishes a range for detecting a heartbeat. On 7 April the New York Post reported that two anonymous sources attributed the officer's location to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) tool called Ghost Murmur. They described quantum magnetic sensing combined with AI that separates a heartbeat signal from background noise. They attributed its development to Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works. Lockheed Martin declined to comment. In a telephone interview with the Post on 8 April, President Trump called the tool important to the rescue but supplied no technical explanation. The Post and Scientific American separately interviewed physicists who questioned the described capability. Ghost Murmur is not named in the official briefing. The briefing establishes no contribution by AI. No public measurements establish that the claimed system located the officer. No inspectable technical account establishes it. On 13 September 2026, 60 Minutes reported from its own interviews that the CIA used top-secret technology to pinpoint the officer's location. CBS did not name Ghost Murmur. It did not say that the technology used AI. Admiral Brad Cooper told CBS that messages from the officer, including “I'm hurt, I'm moving”, reached US forces. The officer said that he carried communication equipment. He said that he did not immediately use it. The documented outcome is one rescued airman, with the claimed AI contribution unverified.
record.purpose: According to the Post's sources, Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works built the tool to find a human heartbeat at a distance, for intelligence collection and personnel recovery. It was tested on Black Hawk helicopters.
record.system: 'Ghost Murmur': long-range quantum (nitrogen-vacancy diamond) magnetometry paired with AI software that isolates heartbeat signatures from background noise, as described by the NY Post's anonymous sources
record.developer: Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, per two NY Post sources; the company declined to comment
record.deployer: US Central Intelligence Agency, per the NY Post; the CIA and White House named no tool

details.value: ABC News, citing Clermont County officials, and WLWT say that the Apple Watch's Crash Detection placed the 911 call. The driver also told WKRC that a Life360 crash-detection service on her mother's phone called police and family. The watch may not have been the only alert. Only news reports are available, and no dispatch log or agency statement is on record.

record.title: After Apple Watch Crash Detection calls 911 for a 19-year-old trapped upside down in her pickup in the Little Miami River, Clermont County crews pull her out with bruises only
record.summary: On 22 February 2026 near Batavia, Ohio, a 19-year-old's truck flipped into the Little Miami River. Clermont County officials say that her Apple Watch Crash Detection called 911. Crews freed her.
record.account: A 19-year-old woman was driving home from work on State Route 222 in Batavia Township, Clermont County, Ohio, on 22 February 2026. According to the Ohio State Highway Patrol accident report cited by ABC News, she lost control on black ice. She hit a tree. She then went off an embankment into the Little Miami River. WLWT says that the truck flipped after dropping down a 15-foot ravine. ABC News (4 March 2026) reports that “According to Clermont County officials, [the driver] was wearing an Apple Watch that automatically called 911 using its crash detection feature”. Body-camera footage released by the Clermont County Sheriff's Office shows a dispatcher keeping her on the line. Central Joint Fire-EMS District firefighters, working with sheriff's deputies, pulled her out after smashing a window. First-year firefighter Tommy Jetter was first into the water. The driver had found a pocket of air of about four inches at the floorboard. According to the accident report, she walked away with bruises. The driver told WKRC (11 March 2026) that there was also “a crash detection on the Live 360 that my mom had on her phone”. She said that it called the police. According to her, it called her family. A second crash-detection service may therefore have placed calls. WLWT and ABC attribute the 911 call to the Apple Watch. Emergency physicians at Okayama University studied records of the Okayama City Fire Bureau. They found that 35 of 49 crash-detection calls from October 2022 to March 2023 were false alarms. They did not examine outcomes for patients.
record.purpose: Apple built Crash Detection to detect a severe car crash from sensor data and call emergency services with the device's location if the wearer does not respond.
record.system: Apple Watch Crash Detection
record.location: Batavia Township, Clermont County, Ohio, United States

ratings.reason: The driver was trapped upside down in a submerged cab in the river at night with an air pocket of about four inches. Crews pulled her out with bruises only, which is a life preserved. The driver told WKRC that a Life360 service on her mother's phone also called police, so no source shows that the watch's call alone brought the crews.
Clermont County dispatch received the automated call and stayed on the line with the driver. The sheriff's office and the fire district have not reported time or resources saved.

ai_role.statement: ABC News, citing Clermont County officials, and WLWT say that the Apple Watch's Crash Detection placed the 911 call. On its support page, Apple says that the feature detects severe crashes from sensor data on the device and calls automatically after a countdown if the wearer does not respond. The driver also told WKRC that a Life360 crash-detection service on her mother's phone called police and family. The watch may not have been the only alert. Only news reports are available, and no dispatch log or agency statement is on record.

fields.summary: On 22 February 2026 near Batavia, Ohio, a 19-year-old's truck flipped into the Little Miami River. Clermont County officials say that her Apple Watch Crash Detection called 911. Crews freed her.
fields.account: A 19-year-old woman was driving home from work on State Route 222 in Batavia Township, Clermont County, Ohio, on 22 February 2026. According to the Ohio State Highway Patrol accident report cited by ABC News, she lost control on black ice. She hit a tree. She then went off an embankment into the Little Miami River. WLWT says that the truck flipped after dropping down a 15-foot ravine. ABC News (4 March 2026) reports that “According to Clermont County officials, [the driver] was wearing an Apple Watch that automatically called 911 using its crash detection feature”. Body-camera footage released by the Clermont County Sheriff's Office shows a dispatcher keeping her on the line. Central Joint Fire-EMS District firefighters, working with sheriff's deputies, pulled her out after smashing a window. First-year firefighter Tommy Jetter was first into the water. The driver had found a pocket of air of about four inches at the floorboard. According to the accident report, she walked away with bruises. The driver told WKRC (11 March 2026) that there was also “a crash detection on the Live 360 that my mom had on her phone”. She said that it called the police. According to her, it called her family. A second crash-detection service may therefore have placed calls. WLWT and ABC attribute the 911 call to the Apple Watch. Emergency physicians at Okayama University studied records of the Okayama City Fire Bureau. They found that 35 of 49 crash-detection calls from October 2022 to March 2023 were false alarms. They did not examine outcomes for patients.

record.title: Lynxight alerts lifeguards at Inglewood Pool to an unconscious swimmer who recovers fully after rescue
record.summary: Lynxight, a camera system at a Perth pool, alerted a lifeguard's smartwatch to a man who had sunk unconscious. Lifeguards rescued him with help from a swimmer. He recovered fully.
record.account: The outdoor pool at Stirling Leisure - Inglewood, Perth, had used Lynxight since a redevelopment ended in September 2024, according to the City of Stirling. On 10 June 2025, a man suffered a medical episode. He sank in the pool. The City of Stirling reports that the lifeguard on patrol did not see the man go under. Lynxight sent lifeguard Cameron Menzies a smartwatch alert giving the swimmer's location, with images. Ofer Lefelman, a swimmer in the pool, independently noticed the emergency. He lifted the man to the surface. Menzies brought him out of the water with fellow lifeguards. The City of Stirling reports that he was conscious when paramedics took him away. It reports that he later recovered fully. 7NEWS reported the rescue on 1 July 2025. ABC News reported on 31 December 2025 that the system was still in use at Inglewood. In that report the city's operations coordinator credited the alert with accelerating the lifeguard's response. ABC reported that Royal Life Saving Australia is studying the system's impact in a research partnership with Lynxight. In the same report, Paul Salmon of the University of the Sunshine Coast asked how pools will prevent over-reliance on the technology, along with the loss of detection skills in lifeguards.

fields.summary: Lynxight, a camera system at a Perth pool, alerted a lifeguard's smartwatch to a man who had sunk unconscious. Lifeguards rescued him with help from a swimmer. He recovered fully.
fields.account: The outdoor pool at Stirling Leisure - Inglewood, Perth, had used Lynxight since a redevelopment ended in September 2024, according to the City of Stirling. On 10 June 2025, a man suffered a medical episode. He sank in the pool. The City of Stirling reports that the lifeguard on patrol did not see the man go under. Lynxight sent lifeguard Cameron Menzies a smartwatch alert giving the swimmer's location, with images. Ofer Lefelman, a swimmer in the pool, independently noticed the emergency. He lifted the man to the surface. Menzies brought him out of the water with fellow lifeguards. The City of Stirling reports that he was conscious when paramedics took him away. It reports that he later recovered fully. 7NEWS reported the rescue on 1 July 2025. ABC News reported on 31 December 2025 that the system was still in use at Inglewood. In that report the city's operations coordinator credited the alert with accelerating the lifeguard's response. ABC reported that Royal Life Saving Australia is studying the system's impact in a research partnership with Lynxight. In the same report, Paul Salmon of the University of the Sunshine Coast asked how pools will prevent over-reliance on the technology, along with the loss of detection skills in lifeguards.

record.title: After AI detects her brain hemorrhage, a nurse returns to nursing following aneurysm treatment
record.summary: Software, apparently Viz.ai, detected a nurse’s brain bleed. It alerted her doctors. After treatment, the nurse returned to full-time nursing.
record.account: A 57-year-old nurse suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm. Her symptoms began on 2 February 2024. Baptist Health gives the date without the year. Jan Engoren’s subsequent interviews with the nurse and her surgeon, Brian Snelling, establish the year. At Baptist Health's Marcus Neuroscience Institute, software analyzed her scan. It alerted clinicians to the bleeding. They sealed the aneurysm with coils delivered through a catheter. After about three weeks in the hospital, she recovered. She returned to full-time nursing. On 29 October 2024, Snelling told CBS12 that the hospital's AI had picked up the nurse's bleeding before any emergency doctor had detected it. No radiologist had detected it yet. On 29 April 2025, The Coastal Star reported that the nurse had returned to full-time work with no lasting effects. That article does not mention AI. The Coastal Star credits her quick action in calling 911, along with the medics who treated her. On 22 October 2025, NeurologyLive published an interview in which the surgeon names Viz.ai. He describes an unnamed intensive care unit nurse whose circumstances match those described here. The product attribution is therefore inferred. The module is not identified in any account. The release is unidentified.

Her symptoms began on 2 February 2024.[1] According to her surgeon, software at Baptist Health's Marcus Neuroscience Institute flagged the bleeding on her scan and alerted clinicians.[2] The clinicians sealed the aneurysm with coils delivered through a catheter. The identification of the software therefore remains an inference.[4] No source isolates what the alert changed for her survival.

record.title: A seizure alert from an Empatica Embrace reaches the mother of a 26-year-old teacher, who calls paramedics after a seizure left her daughter not breathing (Fulton, Missouri)
record.summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that stopped a 26-year-old teacher's breathing. It alerted her mother, who called paramedics. IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
record.account: A 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”, Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018. The article dates the seizure to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics. Dolgin writes that “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. Dolgin writes that the device records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text to pre-specified caregivers. It can call them instead. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The same article reports a case described by Empatica co-founder Rosalind Picard and colleagues, in which the alert reached a 20-year-old's family but nobody arrived for 15 minutes and he died. In a later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021), Empatica staff with hospital co-authors report the sensitivity of a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. In a study in the Montreal epilepsy-monitoring unit that ran the device (Jahani et al. 2026), the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers for 15 of the 16 seizures, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on the IEEE Spectrum article alone. No second account of the event is among the sources.

record.brief: In November 2016 a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure. It left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. The teacher survived. Her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital units where patients with epilepsy are monitored. Researchers in Montreal published a study of the device in their own unit on 7 January 2026. They found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. It raised 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

data.retained_case_account: Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018 on Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri. She “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”. The article dates the seizure to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics, and “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The article says it records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text or call to pre-specified caregivers. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. A later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021) by Empatica staff with hospital co-authors reports sensitivity for a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. An independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study (Jahani et al. 2026) found the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures while worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on this single news item. The Empatica case-study abstract (Regalia, Onorati, Picard, American Epilepsy Society) is not among the sources. No second account of the McGrath event was found.

display.answer: The McGrath rescue rests on the IEEE Spectrum article alone. Empatica is the author of the 510(k) summary filed with the Food and Drug Administration, and Empatica staff are the lead authors of the 2021 study by Onorati et al. The 2026 Montreal study by Jahani et al. Is independent of the maker.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that stopped a 26-year-old teacher's breathing. It alerted her mother, who called paramedics. IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
fields.account: A 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”, Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018. The article dates the seizure to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics. Dolgin writes that “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. Dolgin writes that the device records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text to pre-specified caregivers. It can call them instead. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The same article reports a case described by Empatica co-founder Rosalind Picard and colleagues, in which the alert reached a 20-year-old's family but nobody arrived for 15 minutes and he died. In a later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021), Empatica staff with hospital co-authors report the sensitivity of a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. In a study in the Montreal epilepsy-monitoring unit that ran the device (Jahani et al. 2026), the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers for 15 of the 16 seizures, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on the IEEE Spectrum article alone. No second account of the event is among the sources.

record.title: Diario de Mallorca reports that QP Prostate marked a tiny lesion on a 58-year-old man's MRI at Clínica Girona, a biopsy confirmed cancer, and after surgery he says he is free of disease
record.summary: Diario de Mallorca reports that QP Prostate marked a tiny lesion on a 58-year-old man's MRI at Clínica Girona. A biopsy confirmed cancer, and after surgery he says he is free of disease.
record.account: Quibim, a company in Valencia, makes QP Prostate, an AI assistant that marks likely prostate cancer lesions on MRI. Diario de Mallorca reported on 5 November 2026 that the tool is in use at 12 public hospitals and eight private centers in Spain. At Clínica Girona, it marked a tiny lesion in red on a 58-year-old man's prostate MRI. The radiologist advised a biopsy, which confirmed cancer. The man was operated on nine months before the report. He says that he is now free of disease and credits the AI with finding the tumor when it was tiny. The account is the patient's and the clinic's, and no source says whether radiologists would have found the lesion without the tool.

fields.account: Quibim, a company in Valencia, makes QP Prostate, an AI assistant that marks likely prostate cancer lesions on MRI. Diario de Mallorca reported on 5 November 2026 that the tool is in use at 12 public hospitals and eight private centers in Spain. At Clínica Girona, it marked a tiny lesion in red on a 58-year-old man's prostate MRI. The radiologist advised a biopsy, which confirmed cancer. The man was operated on nine months before the report. He says that he is now free of disease and credits the AI with finding the tumor when it was tiny. The account is the patient's and the clinic's, and no source says whether radiologists would have found the lesion without the tool.

record.title: Saronic's Corsair sea drone carries two Apache crew members off Oman to a helicopter hoist
record.summary: A remotely piloted Saronic Corsair sea drone carried two Apache crew off Oman to a helicopter hoist. Central Command reported that both were rescued within approximately two hours.
record.account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026. That was 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours. It said that they were stable. In its release, Central Command said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew. He said that it carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site. It reported that the vessel located the soldiers. It reported that the vessel carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. Which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue has not been reported. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.
record.purpose: Saronic built the Corsair as an autonomous maritime platform, and Task Force 59 had been fielding it since late March 2026. In this case, the military used it to carry stranded crew members to a point where a helicopter could hoist them.

display.answer: U.S. Central Command describes the rescue in its release of 9 June 2026. Its spokesperson, Captain Tim Hawkins, identified the vessel to DefenseScoop and spoke to Stars and Stripes. Al-Monitor relays what military officials told U.S. Media, and Hegseth's credit of 18 September 2026 comes from the head of the deployer.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: A remotely piloted Saronic Corsair sea drone carried two Apache crew off Oman to a helicopter hoist. Central Command reported that both were rescued within approximately two hours.
fields.account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026. That was 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours. It said that they were stable. In its release, Central Command said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew. He said that it carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site. It reported that the vessel located the soldiers. It reported that the vessel carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. Which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue has not been reported. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.

record.title: A suicide alert from Meta, routed to Uttar Pradesh Police, brings officers to a 25-year-old in Meerut within eight minutes
record.summary: After Meta alerted police to a 25-year-old man's video on Instagram, officers in Meerut reached his home within eight minutes. His condition improved after treatment in hospital.
record.account: On 7 June 2026 a 25-year-old man from the Sardhana area of Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, posted an Instagram video. In it he appeared to drink a white liquid. Police said that Meta sent a suicide alert about the post to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters at 6:53 pm. The center alerted Meerut Police. Then a Sardhana team reached his home within eight minutes. They found him in a critical condition with a bottle of suspected liquid nearby. They took him to hospital, where his condition improved after treatment. He told police that he was under stress following the end of a relationship. According to police data that the Press Trust of India cited, such alerts saved 3,011 lives statewide from 1 January 2023 to 31 May 2026. On 6 January 2026 Decode reported its own interviews with Uttar Pradesh officers. They described rescues. One alert that they described was a false alarm. The outlet noted that Meta publishes no data on false positives for India. On 22 October 2026 the Times of India reported that police credit the alerts with more than 4,000 lives saved from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026.
record.purpose: Meta built the system to flag posts and live videos that show a risk of suicide or self-harm. People review them and, when the danger is close, call emergency services. That is what happened in Meerut.
record.system: Meta proactive self-harm detection on Instagram with alert routing to the Uttar Pradesh Police Social Media Center
record.deployer: Meta Platforms with the Uttar Pradesh Police Social Media Center (agreement signed March 2022)

data.retained_case_account: On 7 June 2026 a 25-year-old man from the Sardhana area of Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, posted an Instagram video. In it he appeared to drink a white liquid. Police said Meta sent a suicide alert about the post to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters at 6:53 pm. The center alerted Meerut Police, and a Sardhana team reached his home within eight minutes. They found him in a critical condition with a bottle of suspected liquid nearby and took him to hospital, where his condition improved after treatment. He told police he was under stress following the end of a relationship. Police data cited by PTI credit such alerts with 3,011 lives saved statewide from 1 January 2023 to 31 May 2026.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: Police sources say Meta sent the alert after the post. They do not state whether Meta's classifier or a user report flagged it. Meta's documentation and NPR describe the process as machine-learning detection with human review before contacting authorities. The record relies on that description and should be read with that caveat.

record.title: When Meta flags a suicide post on Instagram by an 18-year-old in Raebareli at 8:58 pm, Uttar Pradesh Police reach him within 12 minutes after he took rat poison
record.summary: Meta's system for detecting suicide risk flagged an 18-year-old's Instagram post for review. Raebareli police reached him within 12 minutes. He was treated after taking rat poison.
record.account: On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old class 12 student from Raebareli, Uttar Pradesh, texted his girlfriend “Alvida” after a breakup. He lived within the Mill Area police station limits. He posted a suicide video on Instagram with rat poison. The post carried messages of intent. At about 8:58 pm Meta picked out the content. It emailed an alert to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his mobile number. It traced his location. It alerted Raebareli police. A police team reached his home within 12 minutes. They found him in severe distress, with an empty rat-poison packet nearby. Police and family took him to a nearby hospital, where he was treated. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable. A similar rescue after a Meta alert followed in Meerut in June 2026. In October 2026 one followed in Gorakhpur. The Times of India reported on 22 October 2026 that Uttar Pradesh Police say that they saved more than 4,000 lives from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026 by responding to alerts linked to suicide-related posts. According to Decode, the arrangement with Meta has been in place since 2022.
record.purpose: Meta built its detection and review system to find posts and live videos that show a risk of suicide or self-injury. It routes them to trained reviewers and, when the risk is imminent, contacts local authorities. The Uttar Pradesh Police set up their Social Media Center to act on those alerts.

Everything after the email was human work. The center traced the phone number and location. Raebareli police reached the home in 12 minutes on the DGP's instructions, and a hospital treated him.
