record.brief: The Raebareli rescue preceded a similar rescue in Meerut in June 2026. Both took place under an arrangement in which Meta has alerted the Uttar Pradesh Police since 2022.[1] On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old posted a suicide video on Instagram. Meta flagged it at about 8:58 pm and emailed the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his phone number and location and alerted Raebareli police. A team reached his home within 12 minutes and found an empty packet of rat poison. Police and family took him to a hospital. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable.[2] None of the sources says whether Meta’s classifier or a user report first flagged the post.[3] No clinician is quoted, and the type of rat poison is not reported. The claim that his life was saved therefore rests on the police account.[4] Meta’s figure for faster escalation is self-reported and dates from November 2017. At that time, the company said that reports accelerated by pattern recognition were escalated to local authorities twice as quickly as other reports.[5]

fields.account: On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old class 12 student from Raebareli, Uttar Pradesh, texted his girlfriend “Alvida” after a breakup. He lived within the Mill Area police station limits. He posted a suicide video on Instagram with rat poison. The post carried messages of intent. At about 8:58 pm Meta picked out the content. It emailed an alert to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his mobile number. It traced his location. It alerted Raebareli police. A police team reached his home within 12 minutes. They found him in severe distress, with an empty rat-poison packet nearby. Police and family took him to a nearby hospital, where he was treated. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable. A similar rescue after a Meta alert followed in Meerut in June 2026. In October 2026 one followed in Gorakhpur. The Times of India reported on 22 October 2026 that Uttar Pradesh Police say that they saved more than 4,000 lives from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026 by responding to alerts linked to suicide-related posts. According to Decode, the arrangement with Meta has been in place since 2022.

display.answer: The case reports of 1 April 2026 rest on statements by Uttar Pradesh Police, and two of them carry the same IANS story. Decode describes how the arrangement with Meta works, and Meta describes its detection system in newsroom posts of 2017 and 2018. The count of more than 4,000 lives saved is the police's own figure, reported by The Times of India on 22 October 2026.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Meta's system for detecting suicide risk flagged an 18-year-old's Instagram post for review. Raebareli police reached him within 12 minutes. He was treated after taking rat poison.
fields.account: On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old class 12 student from Raebareli, Uttar Pradesh, texted his girlfriend “Alvida” after a breakup. He lived within the Mill Area police station limits. He posted a suicide video on Instagram with rat poison. The post carried messages of intent. At about 8:58 pm Meta picked out the content. It emailed an alert to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his mobile number. It traced his location. It alerted Raebareli police. A police team reached his home within 12 minutes. They found him in severe distress, with an empty rat-poison packet nearby. Police and family took him to a nearby hospital, where he was treated. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable. A similar rescue after a Meta alert followed in Meerut in June 2026. In October 2026 one followed in Gorakhpur. The Times of India reported on 22 October 2026 that Uttar Pradesh Police say that they saved more than 4,000 lives from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026 by responding to alerts linked to suicide-related posts. According to Decode, the arrangement with Meta has been in place since 2022.

record.title: The Kamrup Express stops short of about 60 elephants in Assam after an AI detection system alerts its crew, who also see the herd
record.summary: On 16 October 2024 Northeast Frontier Railway's AI-based Intrusion Detection System alerted the crew of the Kamrup Express, who also saw about 60 elephants crossing in Assam. The crew braked.
record.account: On 16 October 2024 at about 8:37 p.m., train 15959 Kamrup Express was running from Guwahati toward Lumding. It neared a herd of about 60 wild elephants crossing the track between Habaipur and Lamsakhang stations in Assam. Northeast Frontier Railway said that loco pilot J.D. Das and assistant loco pilot Umesh Kumar noticed the herd. It said that they applied the emergency brake. It said that the AI-based Intrusion Detection System operating on that section also alerted the drivers. That system uses existing optical fibers as sensors to identify the movements of animals. Its alerts go to control offices. Station masters get them. Gatemen get them. Loco pilots get them. The train stopped. No collision occurred. Northeast Frontier Railway reported that it saved 414 elephants in 2023 and 383 up to 16 October 2024. By December 2025 the system covered 141 route kilometers of Northeast Frontier Railway. Tenders had been awarded for 981 more route kilometers nationwide. On 20 December 2025 a Rajdhani Express killed seven elephants at Sangjurai, about 30 kilometers away, where the railway said that no such system was installed. The Times of India reported on 21 December 2025 that the system runs on the Habaipur to Lumding section. The paper reported that it covers about 70 kilometers of track in Assam. On 8 October 2026 The Sentinel reported that the railway counted 255 elephants protected in 2026 across four divisions.
record.purpose: The system detects elephants near the track and alerts train drivers and the staff at stations and control rooms. That is what it did in this case.
record.system: AI-based Intrusion Detection System (distributed acoustic sensing on optical fiber), Northeast Frontier Railway

record.title: ASENA analysis program flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives bound for Istanbul
record.summary: The Turkish police's ASENA analysis program flagged a car at Yüksekova on 20 March 2022. Officers found 52.5 kg of explosives. The interior minister said that they were bound for Istanbul.
record.account: On 20 March 2022 at about 19:00, officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at the Yüksekova-Van checkpoint exit in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it as suspicious, initially as a suspected drug shipment. A search of a hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well found 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March that the target was Istanbul. The driver, A.K., a police officer posted in Istanbul, was remanded on 22 March 2022. In a June 2022 interview with Anadolu Ajansı, İbrahim Seydioğulları, head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department, listed the 52 kg of explosives among the finds of operations that he said had started with ASENA. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced A.K. to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. Four co-defendants got 17.5 years each.
record.purpose: The Turkish National Police built ASENA (Analiz Sistemleri Narkotik Ağı) to find and investigate drug crime in linked police and court databases, and it has been in use since March 2021. Police in Hakkari treated the flagged car as a suspected drug shipment, and officers found explosives instead. So this benefit lay outside what the system was built for.

record.developer: Turkish National Police (Emniyet Genel Müdürlüğü), Narcotics Crimes Department; described as written by Turkish engineers, no contractor named

record.brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged the car. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets of factory-made explosive, 52.5 kg in all. The explosive was assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. It sentenced four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for the same offense.[2] ASENA was designed to flag drug crime. This find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs. He said that the police had used analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”.[3] The head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department spoke in June 2022. He listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source records the data that ASENA matched for this car. None of the sources says whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no informant is reported.[5]

display.answer: Hürriyet and Son Dakika report the minister's remarks. The minister credited the police's analysis programs without naming ASENA. Cumhuriyet reports the governorship's statement on the stop. Son Dakika, Demirören Haber Ajansı (DHA) and the Anadolu Ajansı interview with the head of the Narcotics Crimes Department name ASENA. The sentences come from a DHA report that Kısa Dalga republished.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The Turkish police's ASENA analysis program flagged a car at Yüksekova on 20 March 2022. Officers found 52.5 kg of explosives. The interior minister said that they were bound for Istanbul.
fields.account: On 20 March 2022 at about 19:00, officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at the Yüksekova-Van checkpoint exit in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it as suspicious, initially as a suspected drug shipment. A search of a hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well found 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March that the target was Istanbul. The driver, A.K., a police officer posted in Istanbul, was remanded on 22 March 2022. In a June 2022 interview with Anadolu Ajansı, İbrahim Seydioğulları, head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department, listed the 52 kg of explosives among the finds of operations that he said had started with ASENA. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced A.K. to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. Four co-defendants got 17.5 years each.

value.text: ASENA supplied a suspicious-vehicle lead. Officers stopped and searched the car, and forensic and judicial processes established the resulting case.

record.title: After SARUAV detects a lost 65-year-old man lying unconscious in tall grass on drone images, Bieszczady mountain rescuers carry him out alive
record.summary: SARUAV is software that uses convolutional neural networks. On drone images it detected an unconscious 65-year-old man in tall grass after more than 24 hours. Mountain rescuers retrieved him alive.
record.account: On Monday 28 June 2021 at about 4 pm a 65-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease left his home in Cergowa, southeast Poland. He had a stroke the previous day. Police searched with tracking dogs. They did not find him after a storm. On Tuesday 29 June the Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service (GOPR Bieszczady) flew four drone flights. It ran SARUAV on 782 images. SARUAV is software from researchers at the University of Wrocław. It uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to find people in nadir aerial images. After 4 h 31 min of analysis the system detected him and returned his coordinates. He was lying unconscious in grass over two meters tall after more than 24 hours outdoors. GOPR rescuers carried him out. They handed him to the ambulance service. The makers' case report dates the operation to 29 June 2021. Two authors from the Main School of Fire Service in Warsaw wrote in Sustainability in December 2021 that each use of SARUAV needs map data prepared for the area. In 2023, researchers at Texas A&M wrote that SARUAV gives no details on its training data. They wrote that it gives no details on the architecture of its model. The developer's university reports that SARUAV located a second missing person in South Tyrol in August 2024. That person had died. The university reports that rescue services in Europe and Asia now use SARUAV.
record.purpose: Its makers built it to find people in images taken by drones during searches. It did so in this search.

record.brief: The Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service called this the first find in Poland of a missing person using a drone and SARUAV.[1] The missing man was 65. He had Alzheimer's disease and had left home in Cergowa a day after a stroke. Police with tracking dogs did not find him after a storm. On 29 June 2021 the rescue service made four drone flights and ran the SARUAV software on 782 images. After 4 hours and 31 minutes of analysis the software returned his coordinates. Rescuers found him unconscious in grass over two meters tall, after more than 24 hours outdoors. They handed him to the ambulance service. Independent authors wrote that each use of the system needs map data prepared for the area. Other independent authors wrote that SARUAV gives no details on its training data or model architecture.[2] SARUAV Ltd. employs three of the five authors of the case report. The Polish press quotes the rescue service's own account of the find and describes the failed ground search.[3]

data.retained_case_account: On Monday 28 June 2021 at about 4 pm a 65-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease left his home in Cergowa, south-east Poland. He had a stroke the previous day. Police and tracking dogs did not find him after a storm. On Tuesday 29 June the Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service (GOPR Bieszczady) flew four drone flights. It ran SARUAV, software from University of Wrocław researchers that uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to find people in nadir aerial images, on 782 images. After 4 h 31 min of analysis the system detected him and returned his coordinates. He was lying unconscious in grass over two meters tall after more than 24 hours outdoors. GOPR rescuers carried him out and handed him to the ambulance service. The original study explicitly dates the search and rescue operation to June 29, 2021.

fields.account: On Monday 28 June 2021 at about 4 pm a 65-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease left his home in Cergowa, southeast Poland. He had a stroke the previous day. Police searched with tracking dogs. They did not find him after a storm. On Tuesday 29 June the Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service (GOPR Bieszczady) flew four drone flights. It ran SARUAV on 782 images. SARUAV is software from researchers at the University of Wrocław. It uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to find people in nadir aerial images. After 4 h 31 min of analysis the system detected him and returned his coordinates. He was lying unconscious in grass over two meters tall after more than 24 hours outdoors. GOPR rescuers carried him out. They handed him to the ambulance service. The makers' case report dates the operation to 29 June 2021. Two authors from the Main School of Fire Service in Warsaw wrote in Sustainability in December 2021 that each use of SARUAV needs map data prepared for the area. In 2023, researchers at Texas A&M wrote that SARUAV gives no details on its training data. They wrote that it gives no details on the architecture of its model. The developer's university reports that SARUAV located a second missing person in South Tyrol in August 2024. That person had died. The university reports that rescue services in Europe and Asia now use SARUAV.

display.answer: The case report in Remote Sensing and the University of Wrocław press release come from the developer's side. Three of the case report's five authors work for SARUAV Ltd., and one works for the Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service. Three Polish news reports carry the account of GOPR Bieszczady. The 2021 Sustainability study restates the find from the makers' account, and its authors state that they did not test SARUAV themselves.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: SARUAV is software that uses convolutional neural networks. On drone images it detected an unconscious 65-year-old man in tall grass after more than 24 hours. Mountain rescuers retrieved him alive.
fields.account: On Monday 28 June 2021 at about 4 pm a 65-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease left his home in Cergowa, southeast Poland. He had a stroke the previous day. Police searched with tracking dogs. They did not find him after a storm. On Tuesday 29 June the Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service (GOPR Bieszczady) flew four drone flights. It ran SARUAV on 782 images. SARUAV is software from researchers at the University of Wrocław. It uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to find people in nadir aerial images. After 4 h 31 min of analysis the system detected him and returned his coordinates. He was lying unconscious in grass over two meters tall after more than 24 hours outdoors. GOPR rescuers carried him out. They handed him to the ambulance service. The makers' case report dates the operation to 29 June 2021. Two authors from the Main School of Fire Service in Warsaw wrote in Sustainability in December 2021 that each use of SARUAV needs map data prepared for the area. In 2023, researchers at Texas A&M wrote that SARUAV gives no details on its training data. They wrote that it gives no details on the architecture of its model. The developer's university reports that SARUAV located a second missing person in South Tyrol in August 2024. That person had died. The university reports that rescue services in Europe and Asia now use SARUAV.

record.title: Two Tesla Model X cars stopped as a 400-year-old oak fell across the A31 at Sturminster Marshall during Storm Dennis. Eight occupants walked away. One driver credits automatic emergency braking
record.summary: Two Tesla Model X cars stopped as an oak fell across the A31 in Storm Dennis. All eight occupants walked away. One driver credits Autopilot's emergency braking.
record.account: On the evening of Saturday 15 February 2020, during Storm Dennis, a 400-year-old oak fell across the A31 at Sturminster Marshall, Dorset. It hit two Tesla Model X cars going in opposite directions. A man from Brentwood, Essex, was driving his wife and three children to a half-term holiday. The other car was a Tesla loan vehicle driven by a man from Wimborne, with two passengers, a mother and daughter. Both cars stopped suddenly. The Brentwood driver's wife had two black eyes and bruising. Nobody was seriously hurt. That night the Brentwood driver wrote to Tesla and Elon Musk on Twitter: “Autopilot kicked in and saved us.” On 17 February 2020 he told the Mirror that the car was on Autopilot. He said that the emergency braking kicked in. He said that the trunk landed on the hood. On the same day Fred Lambert, the editor in chief of Electrek, questioned the drivers' account. He argued that Tesla's emergency braking could not detect a tree that fell from beside the road. He suggested that the drivers may have braked themselves. He called for the vehicle logs. On 19 February 2020 the Wimborne driver told the Bournemouth Echo that he was not sure whether the car's automatic brakes were enabled. He credited the car's other safety features. The same day the Mirror reported that Elon Musk had replied: “Glad you're all ok.” On 25 February 2020 the Brentwood driver's wife repeated the family's account on BBC London. The sources show no release of the logs by Tesla or the drivers.

data.answer:
Two Model X cars stopped as an oak fell on the A31 in Storm Dennis; eight occupants walked away, both drivers credit the emergency brakes.

One driver credited automatic braking, while the other was unsure whether it was enabled. Without vehicle logs or an engineering reconstruction, the retained accounts cannot establish the braking mechanism or the number of lives that it saved.

By the Brentwood driver's account his car was on Autopilot and the emergency braking stopped it so the trunk hit the bonnet rather than the cabin. The Wimborne driver said he was not sure whether his loan car's automatic brakes were enabled and credited its other safety features. No Tesla data, police finding or engineering assessment of whether either system braked, or whether the drivers would have stopped in time themselves, is reported. Elon Musk's reply, “Glad you're all ok”, acknowledges the outcome, not the mechanism.

data.retained_case_account: On the evening of Saturday 15 February 2020, during Storm Dennis, a 400-year-old oak fell across the A31 at Sturminster Marshall, Dorset. It hit two Tesla Model X cars going in opposite directions. A man from Brentwood, Essex, was driving his wife and three children to a half-term holiday. He told the Mirror the car was on Autopilot, the emergency braking kicked in and the trunk landed on the bonnet. The other car, a Tesla loan vehicle driven by a man from Wimborne with two passengers, a mother and daughter, also stopped suddenly. The Wimborne driver told the Bournemouth Echo he was not sure its automatic brakes were enabled. The Brentwood driver's wife had two black eyes and bruising. Nobody was seriously hurt.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: By the Brentwood driver's account his car was on Autopilot and the emergency braking stopped it so the trunk hit the bonnet rather than the cabin. The Wimborne driver said he was not sure whether his loan car's automatic brakes were enabled and credited its other safety features. No Tesla data, police finding or engineering assessment of whether either system braked, or whether the drivers would have stopped in time themselves, is reported. Elon Musk's reply, “Glad you're all ok”, acknowledges the outcome, not the mechanism.

fields.account: On the evening of Saturday 15 February 2020, during Storm Dennis, a 400-year-old oak fell across the A31 at Sturminster Marshall, Dorset. It hit two Tesla Model X cars going in opposite directions. A man from Brentwood, Essex, was driving his wife and three children to a half-term holiday. The other car was a Tesla loan vehicle driven by a man from Wimborne, with two passengers, a mother and daughter. Both cars stopped suddenly. The Brentwood driver's wife had two black eyes and bruising. Nobody was seriously hurt. That night the Brentwood driver wrote to Tesla and Elon Musk on Twitter: “Autopilot kicked in and saved us.” On 17 February 2020 he told the Mirror that the car was on Autopilot. He said that the emergency braking kicked in. He said that the trunk landed on the hood. On the same day Fred Lambert, the editor in chief of Electrek, questioned the drivers' account. He argued that Tesla's emergency braking could not detect a tree that fell from beside the road. He suggested that the drivers may have braked themselves. He called for the vehicle logs. On 19 February 2020 the Wimborne driver told the Bournemouth Echo that he was not sure whether the car's automatic brakes were enabled. He credited the car's other safety features. The same day the Mirror reported that Elon Musk had replied: “Glad you're all ok.” On 25 February 2020 the Brentwood driver's wife repeated the family's account on BBC London. The sources show no release of the logs by Tesla or the drivers.

record.title: AI software on a Fire and Rescue NSW drone detects two lost hikers off the Dead Horse Gap track, who are located within five hours
record.summary: AI software on a drone of Fire and Rescue NSW flagged two lost hikers in Kosciuszko National Park. They were found within five hours. The fire service has not named the vendor.
record.account: On Tuesday 23 June 2026 two men in their early 20s failed to reach a rendezvous on the Dead Horse Gap walking track. The track is in Kosciuszko National Park, about 35 km southwest of Jindabyne. They were reported overdue at about 7 pm. NSW Police formed an alpine search team with the State Emergency Service. They asked Fire and Rescue NSW for support from drones. Fire and Rescue NSW launched a remotely piloted aircraft with thermal imaging. It carried software that uses AI for detection. The software flagged the pair in bushland about 500 m off the track. The thermal camera confirmed the find. The drone's spotlight directed ground crews to them. They were located less than five hours after the report. They had mild effects of exposure. They declined treatment. Inspector Phillip Eberle of Fire and Rescue NSW later told About Regional that rescuers took about four hours to reach the pair after the find. He said that they guided the pair to safety around midnight. Fire and Rescue NSW described the rescue in a media release on 25 June 2026. On 27 June 2026 ABC News reported that Inspector Eberle said that the technology turned a potential long-term incident into a short-term one. ABC reported that Inspector Eberle said that the technology probably reduced the search by several days. Inspector Russell Turner is the chief remote pilot of Fire and Rescue NSW. He told ABC News that the drones were part of a statewide upgrade of technology introduced over the previous 18 months. ABC reports that this was the first time that Fire and Rescue NSW had used the drone's AI detection to find a missing hiker.
record.purpose: The software finds people, vehicles and boats in images from drones during searches. It found the two hikers.
record.system: Fire and Rescue NSW remotely piloted aircraft system with thermal imaging and AI person-detection software (software vendor not named in the sources)
record.deployer: Fire and Rescue NSW
record.location: Dead Horse Gap track, Kosciuszko National Park, New South Wales, Australia (about 35 km south-west of Jindabyne)

ratings.reason: Two young men lost on a winter night in alpine bushland were found with mild exposure within five hours. The inspector overseeing the search said that it could otherwise have become a long-term incident.
Fire and Rescue NSW, the police and the State Emergency Service avoided an overnight search by several agencies and the risk to rescuers that Inspector Eberle described.

The hikers also signaled with the light of a phone, and the fire service has not named the maker of the software. In its release of 25 June 2026, the fire service confirmed that the AI flagged the pair and that thermal imaging verified the find. It also confirmed that the spotlight guided the rescuers.

data.retained_case_account: On Tuesday 23 June 2026 two men in their early 20s failed to reach a rendezvous on the Dead Horse Gap walking track. The track is in Kosciuszko National Park, about 35 km south-west of Jindabyne. They were reported overdue at about 7 pm. NSW Police formed an alpine search team with the State Emergency Service and asked Fire and Rescue NSW for drone support. FRNSW launched a remotely piloted aircraft with thermal imaging and AI detection software. The software flagged the pair in bushland about 500 m off the track, and the thermal camera confirmed the find. The drone's spotlight directed ground crews to them. They were located less than five hours after the report, had mild effects of exposure and declined treatment. FRNSW Inspector Phillip Eberle said the technology turned a potential long-term incident into a short-term one.

record.title: OpenAI alert relayed through the FBI leads Espírito Santo police to detain a father a day before his stated date to kill his son
record.summary: OpenAI's safety systems flagged a ChatGPT user's plan to kill his 8-year-old son. Alerted through the FBI, Brazilian police held him a day before his stated date.
record.account: In 2026 a 36-year-old farmer in São Gabriel da Palha, Espírito Santo, Brazil, told ChatGPT about a plan to kill his 8-year-old son. He said that he had offered R$50,000 to a hitman. He said that he had set 20 June as the date. OpenAI's safety systems picked out the account. The company referred it to the FBI. The FBI passed it to the Ministry of Justice's CyberLab. The Polícia Civil do Espírito Santo received it on 16 June. It arrested him under warrants on 19 June. Officers seized his phone. They seized four bottles of an unidentified substance. They seized a knotted rope. He admitted the searches but denied intent. He was freed on habeas corpus on 13 August 2026 after 54 days. He wore an ankle monitor. A no-contact order applied to him. The inquiry continues. BBC News Brasil reported on 14 August 2026 that the court freed him because the inquiry had run too long without a charge. display.answer: The police release and the Brazilian news reports of 25 to 27 June 2026 cover the same chain. It ran from OpenAI to the FBI, the Ministry of Justice's CyberLab and the state police, and g1 cites the deputy police chief. BBC News Brasil adds the court's release, the views of legal experts and the lead investigator's account of what OpenAI sent. OpenAI describes the referral process on its policy page of 26 August 2025 and does not mention this case.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: OpenAI's safety systems flagged a ChatGPT user's plan to kill his 8-year-old son. Alerted through the FBI, Brazilian police held him a day before his stated date.
fields.account: In 2026 a 36-year-old farmer in São Gabriel da Palha, Espírito Santo, Brazil, told ChatGPT about a plan to kill his 8-year-old son. He said that he had offered R$50,000 to a hitman. He said that he had set 20 June as the date. OpenAI's safety systems picked out the account. The company referred it to the FBI. The FBI passed it to the Ministry of Justice's CyberLab. The Polícia Civil do Espírito Santo received it on 16 June. It arrested him under warrants on 19 June. Officers seized his phone. They seized four bottles of an unidentified substance. They seized a knotted rope. He admitted the searches but denied intent. He was freed on habeas corpus on 13 August 2026 after 54 days. He wore an ankle monitor. A no-contact order applied to him. The inquiry continues. BBC News Brasil reported on 14 August 2026 that the court freed him because the inquiry had run too long without a charge. Legal experts whom BBC News Brasil interviewed said that the messages justified pretrial detention. They said that the messages alone would not support a charge. The lead investigator told BBC News Brasil that OpenAI sent the user's prompts without ChatGPT's replies.

record.title: Asilla's behavior-analysis AI at about 40 Japanese facilities may have prompted two suicide interventions
record.summary: Asilla says that its behavior-analysis AI for security cameras alerted guards, who reached two people at apparent risk of suicide. The facilities are undisclosed. The dates are undisclosed.
record.account: Tokyo-based Asilla's system assesses the likelihood that a person will jump by analyzing behavior on security-camera footage. Asilla says that it has trained the system since 2022 with around 200 facilities on about seven million pieces of footage. In a product release of 26 January 2024, Asilla describes a function in AI Security asilla version 2.4 that detects the risk of a jump. It uses the trajectories of movement. It uses position. It uses patterns of body motion. The system looks for pacing near a platform edge. It looks for lingering there. It looks for the same behavior on a rooftop. It alerts security guards. It alerts station staff. In some cases it gives loudspeaker warnings. Kyodo reported on 1 June 2026 that about 40 stations and commercial buildings in Japan had introduced the system. It reported that Asilla described two interventions, both undated. In the first the system detected a man loitering in a non-customer area of a commercial facility. A guard found him. He later said that he had intended to kill himself by jumping. In another, a child lingering near an upper-floor railing was found to have been writing a suicide note. Asilla does not say which version was used in these two interventions. All details come from the company via Kyodo. No confirmation from an operator is among the sources. None comes from the police. None comes from an academic.

data.retained_case_account: The two interventions are undated. Tokyo-based Asilla's system assesses the likelihood that a person will jump by analyzing behavior on security-camera footage. It looks for behavior such as pacing or lingering near a platform edge or rooftop. It alerts security guards and station staff, in some cases with loudspeaker warnings. In one case it detected a man loitering in a non-customer area of a commercial facility. A guard found him, and he later said he had intended to kill himself by jumping. In another, a child lingering near an upper-floor railing was found to have been writing a suicide note. Asilla says it trained the system since 2022 with around 200 facilities on about seven million pieces of footage. All details come from the company via Kyodo, and no operator, police or academic confirmation is among the sources. Asilla’s earlier product release identifies a jump-risk detection function in AI Security asilla version 2.4, using movement trajectories, position, and body-motion patterns. It does not identify the version used in these two interventions.

record.summary: Through the FBI, OpenAI disclosed threats that a man wrote in ChatGPT against his ex-girlfriend. He later pleaded guilty to stalking.
record.account: A man wrote threats against his ex-girlfriend in ChatGPT. Court reporting describes an OpenAI emergency disclosure that reached the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office through the FBI. According to the probable cause affidavit cited by the Sun Sentinel, the FBI told the sheriff's office about the messages six days before the arrest. Deputies compared those messages with anonymous threats that the ex-girlfriend had preserved. The woman told detectives that she had not reported the man to police because she did not want to cause his behavior to escalate. The sheriff’s booking entry lists 29 May 2026 as his arrest date. BocaNewsNow reports that he pleaded guilty on 13 August 2026 to written threats. He pleaded guilty to aggravated stalking. He pleaded guilty to unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Adjudication was withheld. He received eight years of probation, including two years of GPS monitoring. The court restricted his contact. It restricted his access to weapons. Reporters cite court documents. They do not reproduce the complete affidavit. They do not reproduce the plea order. Their reports support a police intervention and court restrictions. The sources do not show that an attack would otherwise have occurred.
record.purpose: OpenAI says that when it detects users planning to harm others, it routes the conversations to a small team trained on its usage policies. It says that if human reviewers find an imminent threat of serious physical harm to others, it may refer the case to law enforcement. ChatGPT itself is a general assistant, which the man used to rehearse his plans.

record.title: Frankfurt police find a missing 16-year-old in crisis on Taunusstraße within a day of her disappearance, after a judge-confirmed emergency order let the Bahnhofsviertel camera system's AI search for her face
record.summary: Frankfurt police found a missing 16-year-old in crisis within a day. The face recognition software VAS Videmo360 had flagged her on a Bahnhofsviertel camera, under an order that a judge confirmed.
record.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, which a judge confirmed. The order let the police enter her photograph into the AI-assisted camera system that had run in the district since July 2025. The system operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system showed a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it. A patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody. They returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility. On 16 October 2025 the police announced the rescue. They called it the system's first genuine positive hit. In December 2025 the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) and Doña Carmen sued at the Frankfurt Administrative Court. They asked the court to refer the sections of the police law that allow remote identification to the Federal Constitutional Court. In April 2026 netzpolitik.org reported that police had searched for a low double-digit number of persons with the system since July 2025. This was the only success. By then the Hessian Greens had also asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. In their filing of 22 April 2026 the plaintiffs argue that the law sets no danger threshold for searches for missing persons. In the filing, the plaintiffs cite the police's data protection impact assessment, in which the software is named as VAS Videmo360. By April 2026 the GFF reported that the police had extended the system to two more places in the city center. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.
record.purpose: The Frankfurt police use the AI in the Bahnhofsviertel's Videoschutzanlage to identify people remotely, in real time, from their biometric features. The Hessian police law, amended in February 2025, allows this for narrow purposes such as finding missing persons. In their press release, the police called this case the system's first genuine positive hit.
record.system: AI-assisted video analysis with real-time biometric remote identification in the Frankfurt Bahnhofsviertel police video surveillance system (Videoschutzanlage), monitored from the police Video-Operation-Center
record.model_version: VAS Videmo360 video analysis system (product named in the police data protection impact assessment, as cited in the GFF filing); the police say that only the vendor knows the exact specifications of the face-template model
record.deployer: Polizeipräsidium Frankfurt am Main (Hessian police)

ratings.reason: A 16-year-old whose farewell letter led police to assume an acute psychological crisis was located in the Bahnhofsviertel within a day. She was returned to psychiatric care. fields.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, which a judge confirmed. The order let the police enter her photograph into the AI-assisted camera system that had run in the district since July 2025. The system operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system showed a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it. A patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody. They returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility. On 16 October 2025 the police announced the rescue. They called it the system's first genuine positive hit. In December 2025 the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) and Doña Carmen sued at the Frankfurt Administrative Court. They asked the court to refer the sections of the police law that allow remote identification to the Federal Constitutional Court. In April 2026 netzpolitik.org reported that police had searched for a low double-digit number of persons with the system since July 2025. This was the only success. By then the Hessian Greens had also asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. In their filing of 22 April 2026 the plaintiffs argue that the law sets no danger threshold for searches for missing persons. In the filing, the plaintiffs cite the police's data protection impact assessment, in which the software is named as VAS Videmo360. By April 2026 the GFF reported that the police had extended the system to two more places in the city center. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.

ratings.reason: A 16-year-old whose farewell letter led police to assume an acute psychological crisis was located in the Bahnhofsviertel within a day. She was returned to psychiatric care. The police describe this as averting danger to life and limb. But the police have not said what would otherwise have happened, so their account does not show that a life was saved.

The Frankfurt police recorded the first confirmed success of a system in use since July 2025. The police president and the interior minister cited it as validation. netzpolitik.org reported in April 2026 that it was still the only success among a low double-digit number of searches. The operational gain is modest.

fields.title: Frankfurt police find a missing 16-year-old in crisis on Taunusstraße within a day of her disappearance, after a judge-confirmed emergency order let the Bahnhofsviertel camera system's AI search for her face
fields.headline: Police find a missing 16-year-old after Frankfurt camera AI flags her

fields.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, which a judge confirmed. The order let the police enter her photograph into the AI-assisted camera system that had run in the district since July 2025. The system operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system showed a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it. A patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody. They returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility. On 16 October 2025 the police announced the rescue. They called it the system's first genuine positive hit. In December 2025 the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) and Doña Carmen sued at the Frankfurt Administrative Court. They asked the court to refer the sections of the police law that allow remote identification to the Federal Constitutional Court. In April 2026 netzpolitik.org reported that police had searched for a low double-digit number of persons with the system since July 2025. This was the only success. By then the Hessian Greens had also asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. In their filing of 22 April 2026 the plaintiffs argue that the law sets no danger threshold for searches for missing persons. In the filing, the plaintiffs cite the police's data protection impact assessment, in which the software is named as VAS Videmo360. By April 2026 the GFF reported that the police had extended the system to two more places in the city center. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.

produced_by: A missing-person report with concrete signs of danger to life (a farewell letter) and indications of the person's whereabouts inside the camera-covered district
A legal basis, the Hessian police law amended in February 2025, plus a police-president emergency order confirmed by a judge. These let the girl's photo be entered into the system
An AI-assisted camera network already running in the Bahnhofsviertel since July 2025, with a staffed Video-Operation-Center. Patrols close enough to verify and act on a match the same evening
must_hold: The person passes in front of cameras suitable for automated recognition. netzpolitik.org counted 19 such cameras among the district's 29
A human operator and a patrol verify the automated match before anyone is taken into custody
The search stays within the narrow legal purposes the law allows, which Bild lists as missing persons, kidnapping victims and victims of human trafficking

record.title: Daejeon's AI care robot Kkumdori hears a woman in her 70s, alone at 2 a.m., repeat “I want to die”. She also repeats “save me”. Its alert brings police. She is admitted to hospital
record.summary: Daejeon's Kkumdori care robot, built on ChatGPT 4.0, flagged a woman in her 70s who said “I want to die” at 2 a.m. on 6 August 2025. Police came. She was admitted to hospital the next day.
record.account: On 14 January 2025 Daejeon announced its 2025 program with the company Mr. Mind, which would provide the 1,000 robots. They are its 4.0 model, with conversation based on ChatGPT 4.0. At about 2 a.m. on 6 August 2025, a woman in her 70s identified as “A” was at home in Deogam-dong, Daedeok-gu, Daejeon, South Korea. She lives alone. She has schizophrenia. She has bipolar disorder. She repeatedly told the city-issued AI care robot Kkumdori “I want to die”. She said “save me”. The robot's algorithm for detecting a crisis picked out the words. It alerted the operator's control center. A staff member phoned her. When she kept repeating them, staff reported to police on 112 with her location. Officers found her emotionally unstable. They contacted her family. Police judged hospital treatment urgent. On the afternoon of 7 August she was admitted with her guardian's consent. Daejeon announced the rescue on 13 August 2025. On 10 September 2025 Daejon Ilbo reported that two users that it interviewed value the robot as company. The paper reported that the city acknowledges a gap in use between men and women. Yonhap reported on 1 August 2026 that Daejeon's 1,000 care robots remain in service.
record.purpose: Mr. Mind built the Kkumdori robots to keep people company, remind them of their medicines and schedules and monitor their health. They detect signs of crisis such as suicide risk and depression and notify agencies and guardians automatically. Daejeon issued 1,000 of them from January 2025, 200 per district, to elderly, disabled and low-income people living alone.

ratings.reason: A woman in her 70s living alone, with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, was in acute crisis at 2 a.m. She got a check-in call, a police visit that night and protective hospital admission the next afternoon. The city calls it life-saving, and so do the headlines. No attempt was reported, so the city's account cannot show what would otherwise have happened. Her guardian said that having the robot beside her had been a great support to her.

Daejeon has reported no time, money or capability that its welfare office gained from this case. Its director cited the case as a model, and the city kept the program, but neither is an outcome for the office.

data.retained_case_account: At about 2 a.m. on 6 August 2025, a woman in her 70s identified as “A” was at home in Deogam-dong, Daedeok-gu, Daejeon, South Korea. She lives alone and has schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. She repeatedly told the city-issued AI care robot Kkumdori “I want to die” and “save me”. The robot's crisis-detection algorithm flagged the words and alerted the operator's control center. A staff member phoned her. When she kept repeating them, staff reported to police on 112 with her location. Officers found her emotionally unstable and contacted her family. Police judged hospital treatment urgent. On the afternoon of 7 August she was admitted with her guardian's consent. Daejeon announced the case on 13 August 2025.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The robot's crisis-detection algorithm recognized repeated danger words (“죽고 싶다”, “살려줘”) in conversation at 2 a.m. It sent an alert to a human control center. People did everything after that: the check-in call, the 112 report with location, the police visit, the family contact and the admission. The city's welfare director says the alert is what made the rapid dispatch and protection possible. Whether A would have come to harm that night is not established. Every account derives from the city's 13 August briefing.

display.answer: Most reports restate the city's announcement of 13 August 2025. Daejon Ilbo restated it on 10 September 2025 and added its own interviews with two robot users. Yonhap recounted the case again on 1 August 2026.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Daejeon's Kkumdori care robot, built on ChatGPT 4.0, flagged a woman in her 70s who said “I want to die” at 2 a.m. on 6 August 2025. Police came. She was admitted to hospital the next day.
fields.account: On 14 January 2025 Daejeon announced its 2025 program with the company Mr. Mind, which would provide the 1,000 robots. They are its 4.0 model, with conversation based on ChatGPT 4.0. At about 2 a.m. on 6 August 2025, a woman in her 70s identified as “A” was at home in Deogam-dong, Daedeok-gu, Daejeon, South Korea. She lives alone. She has schizophrenia. She has bipolar disorder. She repeatedly told the city-issued AI care robot Kkumdori “I want to die”. She said “save me”. The robot's algorithm for detecting a crisis picked out the words. It alerted the operator's control center. A staff member phoned her. When she kept repeating them, staff reported to police on 112 with her location. Officers found her emotionally unstable. They contacted her family. Police judged hospital treatment urgent. On the afternoon of 7 August she was admitted with her guardian's consent. Daejeon announced the rescue on 13 August 2025. On 10 September 2025 Daejon Ilbo reported that two users that it interviewed value the robot as company. The paper reported that the city acknowledges a gap in use between men and women. Yonhap reported on 1 August 2026 that Daejeon's 1,000 care robots remain in service.

fields.account: On 14 January 2025 Daejeon announced its 2025 program with the company Mr. Mind, which would provide the 1,000 robots. They are its 4.0 model, with conversation based on ChatGPT 4.0. At about 2 a.m. on 6 August 2025, a woman in her 70s identified as “A” was at home in Deogam-dong, Daedeok-gu, Daejeon, South Korea. She lives alone. She has schizophrenia. She has bipolar disorder. She repeatedly told the city-issued AI care robot Kkumdori “I want to die”. She said “save me”. The robot's algorithm for detecting a crisis picked out the words. It alerted the operator's control center. A staff member phoned her. When she kept repeating them, staff reported to police on 112 with her location. Officers found her emotionally unstable. They contacted her family. Police judged hospital treatment urgent. On the afternoon of 7 August she was admitted with her guardian's consent. Daejeon announced the rescue on 13 August 2025. On 10 September 2025 Daejon Ilbo reported that two users that it interviewed value the robot as company. The paper reported that the city acknowledges a gap in use between men and women. Yonhap reported on 1 August 2026 that Daejeon's 1,000 care robots remain in service.

produced_by: A municipal program that put conversational robots with a crisis-word detection algorithm into 1,000 homes of people living alone, 200 per district, from January 2025.
A 24-hour human control center run by the supplier that receives alerts, phones the resident, and reports to police (112) with the location.
A resident who habitually talked, sang and danced with the robot, so her statements at 2 a.m. were spoken aloud to it.
Police able to attend at night, and a family and hospital able to complete a protective admission the next day.
must_hold: Alerts go to humans who act at night. The robot itself does nothing beyond detecting words and raising the alarm.
The detection catches explicit statements (“죽고 싶다”, “살려줘”). A silent crisis would not trigger it.
Residents keep talking to the device. Her guardian said it was a great support to her.

echoes.setting: Yonhap, 1 August 2026: at about midnight on 20 July 2026 an 80-something in Daejeon's Seo-gu with severe abdominal pain told the care robot to call 119; the control center relayed it, paramedics arrived at about 00:30 and took the person to hospital (https://www.yna.co.kr/view/AKR20260731144200063).
Yonhap, 1 August 2026: in November 2025 an 80-something in Daedeok-gu, badly hurt after falling from bed, called “Aria, help me” to an AI speaker at home and was rescued by 119 (same article).

Daejeon, the same program: a man in his 50s with terminal liver cancer, living alone, was skipping meals. Kkumdori flagged warning signs, and welfare officials visited and arranged meal support (Daejon Ilbo, 10 September 2025).

Daejeon: a woman in her 80s fell at home and could not move. She called for help to an AI speaker, the control center called 119 and she was taken to hospital. Daejeon MBC reported the case on 20 November 2025 without giving its date.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The Seoul Economic Daily and the Korea Herald credit AIID with showing where the man was last seen, and the police team says that its fast route tracking allowed the rescue in time. No source compares the search with and without the system, and the 10-hour figure is a police estimate. Officers still confirmed matches by eye, and the reports do not say how AIID was trained.

record.title: Seoul Economic Daily reports that Anyang police used the AIID system to find a missing man within three hours of the report in June 2025
record.summary: Anyang police used the AIID camera system to narrow the search for a missing man. They found him within three hours of the report. They estimate that a manual search could have taken over 10 hours.
record.account: The Seoul Economic Daily reported on 8 September 2025 that Anyang Dongan Police Station used the AIID system to find a missing man within three hours. In June 2025 a report arrived at 1:24 a.m. that a man had switched off his phone after sending a message that raised fears of suicide. Only one officer of the missing-persons team was available. Dongan district has 2,931 cameras. Officers ran AIID, which showed that the man was last seen in a children's park. Ten officers searched until they found him. The Korea Herald relays the police estimate that a manual search could have taken more than 10 hours. AIID only narrows the search. Officers confirm matches by eye. The police say that privacy rules limit its precision. Anyang City said in October 2025 that police used AIID again to find an 88-year-old with dementia about three hours after the search began. The accounts come from the police, the developer and the city. No outside body measured the result.
record.purpose: Anyang City, the Korea Institute of Science and Technology and the Korean National Police Agency built AIID to find missing people by searching public camera footage and predicting where they went.

ratings.reason: A man who had switched off his phone and sent a message that suggested suicide was found within three hours. The police and the paper describe the rescue as timely, and no source says what harm would otherwise have followed.
The police say that a manual search could have taken more than 10 hours and that AIID narrowed the area for the ten officers who searched. The 10-hour figure is an estimate.

ai_role.statement: The Seoul Economic Daily and the Korea Herald credit AIID with showing where the man was last seen, and the police team says that its fast route tracking allowed the rescue in time. No source compares the search with and without the system, and the 10-hour figure is a police estimate. Officers still confirmed matches by eye, and the reports do not say how AIID was trained.

record.title: AI thermal cameras on a stretch of railway at Madukkarai in Tamil Nadu alert crews, who slow trains for elephants, but a train kills two elephants near Puthuppathi in August 2026
record.summary: The Tamil Nadu Forest Department's AI thermal cameras at Madukkarai sent over 7,116 alerts by 7 July 2026, with no elephant deaths there. A train killed two elephants nearby on 13 August 2026.
record.account: Eleven elephants were killed on the railway tracks of the Madukkarai stretch between 2008 and 2022, the last three in November 2021. Down To Earth reported that the Madras High Court had directed action on elephant deaths on the tracks in 2021. The Tamil Nadu Forest Department installed 24 hybrid thermal cameras with AI detection on 12 towers. They cover 7.05 km of the Ettimadai–Walayar railway section in Madukkarai forest range, Coimbatore district. A trial run had already generated alerts by 7 January 2024. The system has operated since 9 February 2024. Alerts go to a control room at Puthupathi. Its staff warn station masters. They warn loco pilots. They drive elephants away from the tracks. Down To Earth reported on 9 March 2025 that the Tamil Nadu government allocated 7.24 crore rupees for the system. On 21 December 2025 The New Indian Express reported no elephant deaths on the railway tracks of the stretch in the previous 22 months. By 7 July 2026 the department's Additional Chief Secretary reported over 7,116 alerts. The secretary reported 3,281 occasions when trains slowed down or stopped (DT Next reports 3,821). The secretary gave about 9,481 safe crossings by elephants. The official reported no deaths of elephants on the stretch. The department had added AI-powered drones to extend surveillance beyond the fixed cameras. On 13 August 2026 a train killed a mother elephant and her calf near Chavadippara Puthuppathi. The New Indian Express placed the collision on the Tamil Nadu side of the border. The Times of India reported that no warning reached the loco pilot. The New Indian Express placed the collision on the Tamil Nadu side of the border. The Times of India reported that no warning reached the loco pilot. On 31 August 2026 The Hindu reported on a legal notice. According to the notice, this collision occurred on the Walayar-Kanjikode corridor, where a death had occurred in February 2026. The Kerala detection system was still in testing there.

display.answer: The counts of alerts and crossings come from the Forest Department, mostly through statements by its Additional Chief Secretary that news reports reproduce. No official document or log is among the sources. The New Indian Express and The Times of India reported the collision of 13 August 2026. The Hindu reported a legal notice that followed it.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The Tamil Nadu Forest Department's AI thermal cameras at Madukkarai sent over 7,116 alerts by 7 July 2026, with no elephant deaths there. A train killed two elephants nearby on 13 August 2026.
fields.account: Eleven elephants were killed on the railway tracks of the Madukkarai stretch between 2008 and 2022, the last three in November 2021. Down To Earth reported that the Madras High Court had directed action on elephant deaths on the tracks in 2021. The Tamil Nadu Forest Department installed 24 hybrid thermal cameras with AI detection on 12 towers. They cover 7.05 km of the Ettimadai–Walayar railway section in Madukkarai forest range, Coimbatore district. A trial run had already generated alerts by 7 January 2024. The system has operated since 9 February 2024. Alerts go to a control room at Puthupathi. Its staff warn station masters. They warn loco pilots. They drive elephants away from the tracks. Down To Earth reported on 9 March 2025 that the Tamil Nadu government allocated 7.24 crore rupees for the system. On 21 December 2025 The New Indian Express reported no elephant deaths on the railway tracks of the stretch in the previous 22 months. By 7 July 2026 the department's Additional Chief Secretary reported over 7,116 alerts. The secretary reported 3,281 occasions when trains slowed down or stopped (DT Next reports 3,821). The secretary gave about 9,481 safe crossings by elephants. The official reported no deaths of elephants on the stretch. The department had added AI-powered drones to extend surveillance beyond the fixed cameras. On 13 August 2026 a train killed a mother elephant and her calf near Chavadippara Puthuppathi. The New Indian Express placed the collision on the Tamil Nadu side of the border. The Times of India reported that no warning reached the loco pilot. On 31 August 2026 The Hindu reported on a legal notice. According to the notice, this collision occurred on the Walayar-Kanjikode corridor, where a death had occurred in February 2026. The Kerala detection system was still in testing there.

record.title: Apple Watch Fall Detection calling an ambulance for a motorcyclist left unconscious by a hit-and-run in Singapore
record.summary: After a hit-and-run left a Singapore motorcyclist unconscious, Apple Watch Fall Detection called an ambulance. It alerted his girlfriend.
record.account: On the evening of 25 September 2021, a 24-year-old man was riding home when a gray van struck his motorcycle. That was at the junction of Ang Mo Kio Avenue 6 and Ang Mo Kio Street 31, Singapore. The driver fled. The rider lost consciousness on a nearly empty road. His Apple Watch's Fall Detection registered the impact. Via the paired phone it automatically called an ambulance. It texted his emergency contact, his girlfriend. It phoned her. The Singapore Civil Defence Force said that it was alerted around 8:20 p.m. The rider was regaining consciousness as paramedics arrived. He was taken, conscious, to Khoo Teck Puat Hospital. He had abrasions. He wore a neck collar. A bleed at the back of the head was suspected. Police confirmed a hit-and-run.
record.purpose: Apple built Fall Detection to detect a hard fall. If the wearer stays still for about a minute, the watch calls emergency services and sends the location to emergency contacts. Here a motorcycle collision set it off. In its documentation, Apple says only that activity with a high impact may register as a fall.
record.system: Apple Watch Fall Detection
record.model_version: Not reported; Fall Detection requires Apple Watch Series 4 or later (Mothership, citing Apple)

His family call it life-saving, and so does Wanbao in its headline. No clinician or official says so, and a passer-by did reach him, so the sources do not show that it saved his life.

data.retained_case_account: On the evening of 25 September 2021, a 24-year-old man was riding home when a gray van struck his motorcycle. That was at the junction of Ang Mo Kio Avenue 6 and Ang Mo Kio Street 31, Singapore. The driver fled; the rider lost consciousness on a near-empty road. His Apple Watch's Fall Detection registered the impact. Via the paired phone it automatically called an ambulance and texted and phoned his emergency contact, his girlfriend. The Singapore Civil Defence Force said it was alerted around 8:20pm. The rider was regaining consciousness as paramedics arrived. He was conveyed, conscious, to Khoo Teck Puat Hospital with abrasions, a neck collar and a suspected bleed at the back of the head. Police confirmed a hit-and-run.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The watch's fall-detection classifier read the collision's impact as a hard fall. With the wearer unresponsive, it placed the automatic ambulance call through the paired phone and sent the location texts and calls to his girlfriend. SCDF paramedics treated and conveyed him. The counterfactual is unproven. A passer-by later picked up his phone and spoke to the girlfriend. The family at first assumed that person had called the ambulance, and the rider was regaining consciousness as paramedics arrived.

record.title: Odakyu Electric Railway's Panasonic deep-learning “fall detection system” flags a staggering passenger days after it starts on existing cameras at Kyōdō and Soshigaya-Ōkura stations
record.summary: Panasonic's fall detection system at Odakyu alerts staff to people on the tracks. It does the same at the platform edge. The vendor reports that it flagged a staggering passenger on 3 April 2020.
record.account: Pre-learning ran at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line from December 2019. In pre-learning, each camera's detection area was set. The system was taught to distinguish people from trains. On 30 March 2020 Odakyu Electric Railway announced a 転落検知システム (fall detection system) in a press release that Nikkei republished. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. The system would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at both stations, using video from existing station cameras. It was built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan. It applies Panasonic's image-analysis technology to the camera feeds in real time, together with Panasonic's deep-learning technology. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time. Such a person risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. At the launch, Odakyu and Impress Watch reported no detection, no prevented accident and no performance figure. In a case study of September 2020, Panasonic Connect reports a detection on 3 April 2020. The system detected a passenger staggering at the platform edge at Kyōdō. Staff took safety measures. Panasonic says that this prevented an accident. The same case study reports misdetections caused by sunlight. Impress Watch reported on 7 October 2024 a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair users, white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. In its safety reports, Odakyu lists the system as operating at both stations through July 2025. In its report of July 2026, it no longer lists the system. The report shows platform doors installed at Soshigaya-Ōkura, with doors scheduled for Kyōdō in fiscal 2026.
record.purpose: Panasonic and Odakyu built the system to detect people who fall from the platform onto the tracks or linger at the platform edge, and to alert station staff.
record.system: 転落検知システム (fall detection system): Panasonic image-analysis and deep-learning on existing station cameras
record.developer: Panasonic System Solutions Japan, with Odakyu Electric Railway

record.location: Kyōdō and Soshigaya-Ōkura stations, Odakyu Line, Japan

ratings.reason: The vendor reports that the system flagged a passenger staggering at the platform edge at Kyōdō on 3 April 2020 and that staff acted quickly to prevent an accident. The vendor calls it a prevented fall in its heading, and the sources do not show that a train was near, so the rating records a risk removed. The account comes only from the vendor.
The vendor reports that station staff felt more reassured, but it gives no count of alerts, false alarms or staff time.

ai_role.statement: The vendor reports that the deep-learning analysis flagged a staggering passenger and that station staff then took the safety action. So the system raised the alert, and people acted on it. Neither Panasonic nor Odakyu has compared the alerts with what staff watching the cameras would have caught, and the vendor reports misdetections caused by sunlight.

data.retained_case_account: Odakyu Electric Railway announced on 30 March 2020 (press release republished by Nikkei) a 転落検知システム (fall detection system). It would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line. It uses video from existing station cameras. Built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan, the system applies Panasonic's image-analysis and deep-learning technology to analyze the camera feeds in real time. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time and risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. Pre-learning to set each camera's detection area and to distinguish people from trains had run at both stations since December 2019. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. Neither source reports any detection, prevented accident or performance figure, and no later outcome report was found. Impress Watch (7 October 2024) reported a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair and white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. Romanizations of station names are ours; the sources give them in Japanese.

It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. display.answer: Nikkei republished Odakyu's press release of 30 March 2020, and Impress Watch reported the same launch. The detection on 3 April 2020 comes only from Panasonic Connect's case study. The safety reports of 2025 and 2026 are Odakyu's own.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Panasonic's fall detection system at Odakyu alerts staff to people on the tracks. It does the same at the platform edge. The vendor reports that it flagged a staggering passenger on 3 April 2020.
fields.account: Pre-learning ran at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line from December 2019. In pre-learning, each camera's detection area was set. The system was taught to distinguish people from trains. On 30 March 2020 Odakyu Electric Railway announced a 転落検知システム (fall detection system) in a press release that Nikkei republished. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. The system would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at both stations, using video from existing station cameras. It was built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan. It applies Panasonic's image-analysis technology to the camera feeds in real time, together with Panasonic's deep-learning technology. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time. Such a person risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. At the launch, Odakyu and Impress Watch reported no detection, no prevented accident and no performance figure. In a case study of September 2020, Panasonic Connect reports a detection on 3 April 2020. The system detected a passenger staggering at the platform edge at Kyōdō. Staff took safety measures. Panasonic says that this prevented an accident. The same case study reports misdetections caused by sunlight. Impress Watch reported on 7 October 2024 a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair users, white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. In its safety reports, Odakyu lists the system as operating at both stations through July 2025. In its report of July 2026, it no longer lists the system. The report shows platform doors installed at Soshigaya-Ōkura, with doors scheduled for Kyōdō in fiscal 2026.

record.title: Apple Watch Fall Detection calls 911 after a 28-year-old hiker falls from a ledge in Hartshorne Woods Park, New Jersey
record.summary: On 14 October 2019 a lost hiker fell about 30 feet in Hartshorne Woods Park, New Jersey. His new Apple Watch's Fall Detection called 911. It texted his family with his location.
record.account: A 28-year-old man got lost with his hiking companion in Hartshorne Woods Park, Monmouth County, New Jersey. It was 14 October 2019, as darkness fell. They slid down a steep slope onto a ledge. Police said that they fell about 30 feet (NBC News, 23 October 2019). He had bought the watch two days earlier. He had turned on Fall Detection while exploring its settings. He told NBC New York that he heard “911, what's your emergency” from the watch. The watch texted his mother with his location. It texted his sister. His mother drove to the park. “Three agencies responded, according to Middletown police”. A civilian boater brought the pair to safety. NBC News reports a fractured back. It reports leg injuries. It reports foot injuries. ABC7 New York reports a fracture to his right hand. The Associated Press reports undisclosed injuries. No police report has been found. No dispatch record has been found.

record.title: After the SkinVision app rated a changing mole on a man's arm high risk, a biopsy showed stage 1A melanoma
record.summary: SkinVision rated a changing mole on a 31-year-old's arm high risk. A stage 1A melanoma was found and removed, and he is cancer-free.
record.account: A 31-year-old office worker from Liverpool living in Vauxhall, South London, noticed a new 1 cm mole on his left arm in March 2018. He did not see a doctor. Twelve months later the mole turned pink. He checked it with SkinVision, an app that uses artificial intelligence to grade photographed moles as low, medium or high risk. The app returned a high-risk rating and urged him to see a doctor. His general practitioner referred him to a dermatologist. Two weeks later the mole was removed in a 40-minute operation. The biopsy showed stage 1A melanoma. A further biopsy found no spread. He is cancer-free. The Daily Mail reported the story on 17 January 2020. It gave no date for the check with the app. It gave none for the surgery. Researchers report mixed results for the app. The authors of a BMJ systematic review published on 10 February 2020 found a sensitivity of 80% across three small studies. They warned that such apps cannot be relied on to detect all skin cancers. In a study published on 4 February 2022 and funded by a research grant from SkinVision, Erasmus MC researchers found that the app rated 86.9% of premalignant and malignant lesions high risk. In a study published on 7 August 2022, researchers at the university hospitals of Basel and Zurich tested app version 6.8.1. They found that the app rated far more lesions high risk than dermatologists did, with a sensitivity of 41.3% to 83.3% for melanoma.
record.purpose: SkinVision built the app to grade a phone photograph of a mole as low, medium or high risk. It tells users with a high-risk result to see a doctor, and it sends advice from a dermatologist within 48 hours. That is how he used it.
record.system: SkinVision skin-check app (AI analysis of smartphone photographs of moles, graded low, medium or high risk)

ratings.reason: A biopsy-confirmed stage 1A melanoma was excised, further tests found no spread and he is reported cancer-free. He calls it life-saving, but stage 1A is early disease and no clinician is quoted on prognosis. How long he would otherwise have waited is his own estimate.

The change of color alone had not. He said he only goes to the doctor when absolutely desperate. The referral, excision, biopsy and staging were done by the GP, the dermatologist and pathology, none of whom the Daily Mail quotes. The Daily Mail reports neither the app's score nor its version, or whether he used the dermatologist advice within 48 hours that it mentions.

fields.account: A 31-year-old office worker from Liverpool living in Vauxhall, South London, noticed a new 1 cm mole on his left arm in March 2018. He did not see a doctor. Twelve months later the mole turned pink. He checked it with SkinVision, an app that uses artificial intelligence to grade photographed moles as low, medium or high risk. The app returned a high-risk rating and urged him to see a doctor. His general practitioner referred him to a dermatologist. Two weeks later the mole was removed in a 40-minute operation. The biopsy showed stage 1A melanoma. A further biopsy found no spread. He is cancer-free. The Daily Mail reported the story on 17 January 2020. It gave no date for the check with the app. It gave none for the surgery. Researchers report mixed results for the app. The authors of a BMJ systematic review published on 10 February 2020 found a sensitivity of 80% across three small studies. They warned that such apps cannot be relied on to detect all skin cancers. In a study published on 4 February 2022 and funded by a research grant from SkinVision, Erasmus MC researchers found that the app rated 86.9% of premalignant and malignant lesions high risk. In a study published on 7 August 2022, researchers at the university hospitals of Basel and Zurich tested app version 6.8.1. They found that the app rated far more lesions high risk than dermatologists did, with a sensitivity of 41.3% to 83.3% for melanoma.

fields.summary: SkinVision rated a changing mole on a 31-year-old's arm high risk. A stage 1A melanoma was found and removed, and he is cancer-free.
fields.account: A 31-year-old office worker from Liverpool living in Vauxhall, South London, noticed a new 1 cm mole on his left arm in March 2018. He did not see a doctor. Twelve months later the mole turned pink. He checked it with SkinVision, an app that uses artificial intelligence to grade photographed moles as low, medium or high risk. The app returned a high-risk rating and urged him to see a doctor. His general practitioner referred him to a dermatologist. Two weeks later the mole was removed in a 40-minute operation. The biopsy showed stage 1A melanoma. A further biopsy found no spread. He is cancer-free. The Daily Mail reported the story on 17 January 2020. It gave no date for the check with the app. It gave none for the surgery. Researchers report mixed results for the app. The authors of a BMJ systematic review published on 10 February 2020 found a sensitivity of 80% across three small studies. They warned that such apps cannot be relied on to detect all skin cancers. In a study published on 4 February 2022 and funded by a research grant from SkinVision, Erasmus MC researchers found that the app rated 86.9% of premalignant and malignant lesions high risk. In a study published on 7 August 2022, researchers at the university hospitals of Basel and Zurich tested app version 6.8.1. They found that the app rated far more lesions high risk than dermatologists did, with a sensitivity of 41.3% to 83.3% for melanoma.
