record.title: After Taichung's AI smoke-recognition system flags a man who repeatedly burned roadside waste in Dadu District, police identify him
record.summary: The Taichung Environmental Protection Bureau's AI smoke-recognition system flagged the burning of roadside waste in Dadu District. Police identified a 74-year-old repeat burner, who faces a fine.
record.account: In March 2025 Taichung's Environmental Protection Bureau received a complaint about smoke from a dumping spot beside Hugan Road, Dadu District. The bureau then installed its system that recognizes smoke with AI at the site. It installed air micro-sensors. It installed cameras. The Central News Agency reports that shortly after 08:00 on 4 July 2025 the instruments showed abnormal air quality. Inspectors found dumped waste burning. The system recorded the same man in July and August. His motorcycle plate was too faded to read. So inspectors collected neighbors' closed-circuit television footage. They collected dashcam footage. A Wuri Precinct officer recognized a 74-year-old man, who confessed. On 13 September 2025 the bureau announced a fine of up to NT$100,000 under the Air Pollution Control Act. It asked the land manager to clear the site. The bureau told Public Television Service that the site already had cameras, which may have had blind spots. It said that the dumped waste had built up over a long time. On 26 February 2026 the United Daily News reported the bureau's own figures for the whole program. Alerts for open burning had fallen 59.7 percent. Complaints had fallen 43.4 percent. By August 2026 the bureau reported nearly 170 AI smoke-detection systems across Taichung.
record.purpose: The bureau introduced AI smoke-recognition cameras in 2022 to detect abnormal smoke around the clock at hotspots of open burning. They send automatic alerts so that inspectors can find and stop sources of pollution and reduce the risk of fire.
record.system: AI智慧判煙系統 (AI smart smoke-recognition system) with air micro-sensors and surveillance cameras, operated by the Taichung City Environmental Protection Bureau; 36 hotspot monitoring stations as of July 2025 and over 100 AI and sensor sites citywide by September 2025
record.deployer: Taichung City Government Environmental Protection Bureau (臺中市政府環境保護局)

ratings.reason: The bureau says that the case removed “a potential pollution source threatening air quality” for residents near Hugan Road in Dadu District. Reporters at Chinese Television System and Public Television Service describe repeated burns at the same spot, next to weeds, in February, July and August 2025. No exposure figures or air-quality measurements are reported. The benefit is therefore material but local and unquantified.

The bureau and the Wuri Precinct police solved a case of repeated burning that had stalled because the motorcycle plate was too faded to read. The system's alert sent inspectors to the site, and its video supplied the core evidence. The bureau presents the case as proof that its “smart technology city” enforcement works.

ai_role.statement: The AI smoke-recognition system and micro-sensors supplied the detection that sent inspectors to the burning site. CNA dates it first to 4 July 2025, then repeatedly in July and August. It also supplied the video that recorded the offender. It could not read his faded motorcycle plate. So identification came from private CCTV, dashcam footage and a police officer's recognition of a local resident. The system's contribution is detection and documentation. Removal of the source depended on human investigation. No change in air quality was measured, and the bureau has not shown what would otherwise have happened.

data.retained_case_account: Taichung's Environmental Protection Bureau (EPB) installed its AI smoke-recognition system, air micro-sensors and cameras beside Hugan Road, Dadu District. That followed a March 2025 complaint about smoke from a dumping spot. CNA reports that shortly after 08:00 on 4 July 2025 the instruments flagged abnormal air quality. Inspectors found dumped waste burning. The system recorded the same man in July and August. His motorcycle plate was too faded to read. So inspectors collected neighbors' closed-circuit television (CCTV) and dashcam footage. A Wuri Precinct officer recognized a 74-year-old man, who confessed. On 13 September 2025 the EPB announced a fine of up to NT$100,000 under the Air Pollution Control Act. It asked the land manager to clear the site.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The AI smoke-recognition system and micro-sensors supplied the detection that sent inspectors to the burning site. CNA dates it first to 4 July 2025, then repeatedly in July and August. It also supplied the video that recorded the offender. It could not read his faded motorcycle plate. So identification came from private CCTV, dashcam footage and a police officer's recognition of a local resident. The system's contribution is detection and documentation. Removal of the source depended on human investigation. No measured air-quality change or proven counterfactual is reported. So the record sits at protective response with prevention unproven rather than specific harm prevented.

fields.summary: The Taichung Environmental Protection Bureau's AI smoke-recognition system flagged the burning of roadside waste in Dadu District. Police identified a 74-year-old repeat burner, who faces a fine.
fields.account: In March 2025 Taichung's Environmental Protection Bureau received a complaint about smoke from a dumping spot beside Hugan Road, Dadu District. The bureau then installed its system that recognizes smoke with AI at the site. It installed air micro-sensors. It installed cameras. The Central News Agency reports that shortly after 08:00 on 4 July 2025 the instruments showed abnormal air quality. Inspectors found dumped waste burning. The system recorded the same man in July and August. His motorcycle plate was too faded to read. So inspectors collected neighbors' closed-circuit television footage. They collected dashcam footage. A Wuri Precinct officer recognized a 74-year-old man, who confessed. On 13 September 2025 the bureau announced a fine of up to NT$100,000 under the Air Pollution Control Act. It asked the land manager to clear the site. The bureau told Public Television Service that the site already had cameras, which may have had blind spots. It said that the dumped waste had built up over a long time. On 26 February 2026 the United Daily News reported the bureau's own figures for the whole program. Alerts for open burning had fallen 59.7 percent. Complaints had fallen 43.4 percent. By August 2026 the bureau reported nearly 170 AI smoke-detection systems across Taichung.

The Central News Agency reports that shortly after 08:00 on 4 July 2025 the instruments showed abnormal air quality. Inspectors found dumped waste burning. It asked the land manager to clear the site. The bureau told Public Television Service that the site already had cameras, which may have had blind spots. It said that the dumped waste had built up over a long time. On 26 February 2026 the United Daily News reported the bureau's own figures for the whole program. produced_by: Fixed AI smoke-recognition cameras and air micro-sensors installed at a known open-burning hotspot after a public complaint, with automatic alerts to inspectors
Inspectors able to reach the site while the fire burned. They could assemble third-party CCTV and dashcam footage when its video could not read the faded plate
Local police (Wuri Precinct Dadu Station) familiar enough with residents to match the recorded build, clothing and gait to a known 74-year-old resident
A legal basis for penalties (Air Pollution Control Act Article 32) and a land manager that could be asked to clear the dump site
must_hold: The AI alert must reach staff who can respond while the fire is burning and who have the mandate to enter the site
Identification must not rest on the camera alone. Plate recognition failed here and human evidence-gathering closed the case
The offender must be identifiable and reachable. A stranger with no local ties would likely not have been recognized

record.title: Android Earthquake Alerts warns more than 16 million users of the Marmara Ereğlisi earthquake on 23 April 2025
record.summary: Google's Android Earthquake Alerts detected the Marmara Ereğlisi earthquake of 23 April 2025. It alerted over 16 million users, but its stronger alert missed inland areas of moderate shaking.
record.account: On 23 April 2025 the Marmara Ereğlisi earthquake, of moment magnitude (Mw) 6.2, struck offshore in the Sea of Marmara, Türkiye. Initial reports cited by the evaluation put shaking in Istanbul at intensity V on the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale. At least 359 people were injured, mostly from panic. Google's Android Earthquake Alerts (AEA) system uses the accelerometers of online Android phones. Google launched it in Türkiye in June 2021. An on-phone detection algorithm flags sudden changes in acceleration. The system detected the event 5.31 seconds after its origin. It issued a first “Be Aware” alert 0.43 seconds later on an initial magnitude estimate of Mw 4.83. “Take Action” alerts followed as the estimate rose. Alerts reached more than 16 million Android users in Türkiye, Greece, Romania and Bulgaria. For residents in correctly alerted geographic areas of weak shaking (MMI III), modeled warning times reached up to 150 seconds. Their median was 56 seconds. The rate of true positives was 90%. Precision was 99%. Both figures count people by geographic area. They do not count alerted devices. In a separate voluntary survey of 67,056 recipients, 50.5% reported receiving a warning before they felt shaking. The final magnitude estimate saturated at Mw 6.04, so the “Take Action” polygon was too small. Inland populations that felt MMI V shaking received only the “Be Aware” warning before stronger shaking arrived. Google reports that more than 116 million alerts had been issued in Türkiye for 203 detected events between June 2021 and 16 September 2025. Google employees wrote the system description (Science, 17 July 2025). They wrote the evaluation (Nature Communications, 11 August 2026). The data from user feedback come from Google. The same system underestimated the Türkiye earthquakes of 6 February 2023. The BBC reported on 27 July 2025 that only 469 “Take Action” alerts were sent for the magnitude 7.8 event, when 10 million people could have received one.
record.purpose: Google built the system to detect earthquakes with the accelerometers of Android phones and send early warnings, in countries without dense seismic networks.
record.system: Android Earthquake Alerts (AEA) system
record.deployer: Google (alerts delivered directly to Android users; launched in Türkiye in June 2021)
record.location: Sea of Marmara / Istanbul region, Türkiye (alerts also in Greece, Romania and Bulgaria)

ratings.reason: By Google's feedback data, recipients were likely to drop, cover and hold on or to warn others. No individual injury avoided is documented, and Google collected the data.
No organization's decision or operation is documented as changed by the alerts.

More than 16 million users were alerted, with a median warning of 56 seconds for weak shaking. The “Take Action” alerts did not reach inland areas of moderate shaking (MMI V) in time. No reduction in injuries is demonstrated, and Google employees wrote the evidence.

fields.account: On 23 April 2025 the Marmara Ereğlisi earthquake, of moment magnitude (Mw) 6.2, struck offshore in the Sea of Marmara, Türkiye. Initial reports cited by the evaluation put shaking in Istanbul at intensity V on the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale. At least 359 people were injured, mostly from panic. Google's Android Earthquake Alerts (AEA) system uses the accelerometers of online Android phones. Google launched it in Türkiye in June 2021. An on-phone detection algorithm flags sudden changes in acceleration. The system detected the event 5.31 seconds after its origin. It issued a first “Be Aware” alert 0.43 seconds later on an initial magnitude estimate of Mw 4.83. “Take Action” alerts followed as the estimate rose. Alerts reached more than 16 million Android users in Türkiye, Greece, Romania and Bulgaria. For residents in correctly alerted geographic areas of weak shaking (MMI III), modeled warning times reached up to 150 seconds. Their median was 56 seconds. The rate of true positives was 90%. Precision was 99%. Both figures count people by geographic area. They do not count alerted devices. In a separate voluntary survey of 67,056 recipients, 50.5% reported receiving a warning before they felt shaking. The final magnitude estimate saturated at Mw 6.04, so the “Take Action” polygon was too small. Inland populations that felt MMI V shaking received only the “Be Aware” warning before stronger shaking arrived. Google reports that more than 116 million alerts had been issued in Türkiye for 203 detected events between June 2021 and 16 September 2025. Google employees wrote the system description (Science, 17 July 2025). They wrote the evaluation (Nature Communications, 11 August 2026). The data from user feedback come from Google. The same system underestimated the Türkiye earthquakes of 6 February 2023. The BBC reported on 27 July 2025 that only 469 “Take Action” alerts were sent for the magnitude 7.8 event, when 10 million people could have received one.

fields.summary: Google's Android Earthquake Alerts detected the Marmara Ereğlisi earthquake of 23 April 2025. It alerted over 16 million users, but its stronger alert missed inland areas of moderate shaking.
fields.account: On 23 April 2025 the Marmara Ereğlisi earthquake, of moment magnitude (Mw) 6.2, struck offshore in the Sea of Marmara, Türkiye. Initial reports cited by the evaluation put shaking in Istanbul at intensity V on the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale. At least 359 people were injured, mostly from panic. Google's Android Earthquake Alerts (AEA) system uses the accelerometers of online Android phones. Google launched it in Türkiye in June 2021. An on-phone detection algorithm flags sudden changes in acceleration. The system detected the event 5.31 seconds after its origin. It issued a first “Be Aware” alert 0.43 seconds later on an initial magnitude estimate of Mw 4.83. “Take Action” alerts followed as the estimate rose. Alerts reached more than 16 million Android users in Türkiye, Greece, Romania and Bulgaria. For residents in correctly alerted geographic areas of weak shaking (MMI III), modeled warning times reached up to 150 seconds. Their median was 56 seconds. The rate of true positives was 90%. Precision was 99%. Both figures count people by geographic area. They do not count alerted devices. In a separate voluntary survey of 67,056 recipients, 50.5% reported receiving a warning before they felt shaking. The final magnitude estimate saturated at Mw 6.04, so the “Take Action” polygon was too small. Inland populations that felt MMI V shaking received only the “Be Aware” warning before stronger shaking arrived. Google reports that more than 116 million alerts had been issued in Türkiye for 203 detected events between June 2021 and 16 September 2025. Google employees wrote the system description (Science, 17 July 2025). They wrote the evaluation (Nature Communications, 11 August 2026). The data from user feedback come from Google. The same system underestimated the Türkiye earthquakes of 6 February 2023. The BBC reported on 27 July 2025 that only 469 “Take Action” alerts were sent for the magnitude 7.8 event, when 10 million people could have received one.

value.text: The service automatically detected the event and issued updated warnings directly to phones, and recipients chose how to respond.

record.title: The Karnataka Examinations Authority's facial recognition app exposes a woman who tried to take a Bengaluru entrance exam on another candidate's forged admit card
record.summary: The Karnataka Examinations Authority's facial recognition app flagged a woman with a forged admit card for an entrance test in Bengaluru on 17 April 2025. She fled before writing the paper.
record.account: On Thursday 17 April 2025 a woman tried to enter the mathematics paper of the 2025 Common Entrance Test. The center was Silver Valley Public PU College in Malleswaram, Bengaluru. She had spent nearly an hour in the restroom. Her admit card carried her own pasted photograph. The name on it was altered. It bore the hall ticket number and QR code of a genuine candidate. Staff scanned the code. They captured her photo with the new facial recognition app of the Karnataka Examinations Authority. The app marked her as someone other than the registered candidate. She fled before the principal was told. H. Prasanna, the authority's executive director, ordered a report with video footage. He said that legal action would follow. The authority kept facial recognition for every candidate at the 2026 Common Entrance Test on 23 and 24 April 2026. It kept the QR-code checks. On 31 July 2026 Prasanna said that candidates for the civil police constable recruitment exam of 2 August 2026 would enter only after facial recognition verification.
record.purpose: The Karnataka Examinations Authority built the app to verify candidates at the hall entrance and prevent impersonation. It scans the admit card's QR code and matches a live photograph against the photo submitted at registration.
record.system: Karnataka Examinations Authority QR code-based facial recognition app (CET-2025 candidate verification)
record.developer: Karnataka Examinations Authority (The Hindu and ETV Bharat: 'developed by KEA'; no vendor named)
record.deployer: Karnataka Examinations Authority

ratings.reason: KEA stopped an attempt to enter with forged papers in the app's first statewide run. The Hindu reports that all verifications ran without technical glitches on the second day. The authority gained a working check on identity across 3,30,808 registrants, shown in one case.

One person who was not the candidate on record was kept out of the test. The exam authority has not reported an effect on the 3.3 lakh registrants or what she meant to gain. So the extent of any benefit to the cohort cannot be established.

It “revealed that she was not the genuine candidate” (The Hindu). The Hindu and the Times of India both report the forged card's contents. It carried her own photograph with the genuine candidate's hall ticket number and QR code. Comparing the card with her face would therefore not have exposed her. The flag depended on the app's match against the registered photograph. Staff then acted, but she fled before the principal was told. No arrest or sanction is attributable to the system. KEA's probe and the promised legal action were still pending in every report.

produced_by: Admit cards printed with a QR code that resolves to the candidate's registered record and photograph. A photo pasted over the card therefore does not change what the app compares against.
A live photograph taken at the hall door and matched by the app against the registered photo before entry. This ran at every center rather than the earlier pilot subset.
Center staff instructed to act on a mismatch and escalate to the principal and KEA. Video coverage of the entrance that KEA could call for afterwards.
must_hold: The registered photograph must be of the genuine candidate. The control fails if the fraud is committed at registration rather than at the door.
Verification must be completed before the candidate is admitted. This depends on staffing and app reliability at scale. KEA reported no glitches this time.
A flagged person must be detained or identified on the spot. Here she fled, so the deterrent rests on the probe and the video footage rather than on an arrest.

details.value: ASENA picked the car, and the dog Hector and the officers found the drugs and made the arrests. In 2022 the Interior Minister declined to give details of how ASENA works. record.account: In May 2022 Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said that ASENA starts following people who go to a province for the first time. He said that it follows people who take a route for the first time. People who stay at a hotel for the first time are followed. He claimed that it had helped solve 3,593 cases. In March 2025 Şırnak Provincial Police stopped a vehicle at the Köy Hizmetleri (Village Services) police checkpoint after ASENA selected it for inspection. DHA calls ASENA police software “in artificial intelligence format”. The narcotics dog Hector then found 86 kilograms 600 grams of skunk in 119 packages hidden in the trunk. Three occupants, M.E., H.K. and Ş.A., were detained (Sözcü/DHA and Habertürk/DHA, 17 March 2025). fields.summary: Şırnak police stopped a car that the ASENA narcotics software had selected. In March 2025 the dog Hector found 86.6 kg of skunk in 119 packages in the trunk. Three lawyers were remanded.
fields.account: In May 2022 Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said that ASENA starts following people who go to a province for the first time. He said that it follows people who take a route for the first time. People who stay at a hotel for the first time are followed. He claimed that it had helped solve 3,593 cases. In March 2025 Şırnak Provincial Police stopped a vehicle at the Köy Hizmetleri (Village Services) police checkpoint after ASENA selected it for inspection. DHA calls ASENA police software “in artificial intelligence format”. The narcotics dog Hector then found 86 kilograms 600 grams of skunk in 119 packages hidden in the trunk. Three occupants, M.E., H.K. and Ş.A., were detained (Sözcü/DHA and Habertürk/DHA, 17 March 2025). Diken, citing İHA, gives ASENA's full name as Analiz Sistemleri Narkotik Ağı (Narcotics Analysis Systems Network). It says that the three were lawyers registered with the Mardin Bar Association. They were taken to court after police processing. They were remanded in custody (Diken, 18 March 2025). The day of the stop is unreported. No report gives the data that ASENA analyzed. How it chose the car is not reported. Rudaw, relaying the Şırnak Provincial Police Directorate's statement, says that police teams assessing a tip stopped the vehicle. No official is named. The case against the three lawyers has no reported outcome after the remand that Diken reported on 18 March 2025. Rûdaw, citing the provincial police directorate's statement, wrote that teams evaluating a tip stopped the vehicle at the checkpoint, and it does not mention ASENA.

record.title: A facial recognition check at an Adana police stop identified a man who said that he had no identity document as a robbery convict wanted to serve a sentence of 10 years, 1 month and 10 days
record.summary: A police facial recognition system matched a man stopped in Adana without identification to a robbery convict wanted to serve a 10-year sentence. No report gives the system's name.
record.account: Officers of the Seyhan District Police Directorate in Adana, Turkey, stopped a suspicious man during a street check in the Sucuzade neighborhood. He said that he had no identity document. By the account of the Demirören News Agency (DHA), he gave contradictory statements. So the district's Crime Prevention and Investigation Bureau took him to the station to check his fingerprints. The bureau ran a check with facial recognition. The facial recognition system matched him to a 38-year-old fugitive convict wanted to serve 10 years, 1 month and 10 days for robbery. DHA said that he would go to prison once processing was done. The İhlas News Agency (İHA) and DHA published this in the early hours of 4 March 2025 without stating the day of the stop.
record.purpose: Police use facial recognition to check people against records of identity and of wanted people. Here it matched a detainee with no identification to a fugitive convict.
record.system: Facial recognition system used by Turkish police at the Seyhan district station (not named in the reports)
record.deployer: Seyhan District Police Directorate, Adana (Turkish National Police)
record.segment: Street identity checks by district police

ratings.reason: The Seyhan unit established at the station that a man who said that he had no identity document and gave contradictory statements was a fugitive convict. He had a robbery sentence of 10 years, 1 month and 10 days outstanding, and could go to prison. The gain was material and confined to a single case for one police unit.
One convicted robber who had evaded a long sentence was returned to custody. The police have not reported that further harm was prevented, so the public benefit is small and diffuse.

fields.account: Officers of the Seyhan District Police Directorate in Adana, Turkey, stopped a suspicious man during a street check in the Sucuzade neighborhood. He said that he had no identity document. By the account of the Demirören News Agency (DHA), he gave contradictory statements. So the district's Crime Prevention and Investigation Bureau took him to the station to check his fingerprints. The bureau ran a check with facial recognition. The facial recognition system matched him to a 38-year-old fugitive convict wanted to serve 10 years, 1 month and 10 days for robbery. DHA said that he would go to prison once processing was done. The İhlas News Agency (İHA) and DHA published this in the early hours of 4 March 2025 without stating the day of the stop.

ratings.reason: The Seyhan unit established at the station that a man who said that he had no identity document and gave contradictory statements was a fugitive convict. He had a robbery sentence of 10 years, 1 month and 10 days outstanding, and could go to prison. The gain was material and confined to a single case for one police unit.
One convicted robber who had evaded a long sentence was returned to custody. The police have not reported that further harm was prevented, so the public benefit is small and diffuse.

record.title: CGU's ALICE robot flags overpricing in three tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro in 2024, two of which are stopped while the third is re-estimated
record.summary: ALICE, a tool of the CGU, flagged three 2024 tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state. Auditors confirmed R$19.4m of overpricing risk. Two tenders were stopped. The third was re-estimated.
record.account: In March 2023 Fernanda Odilla of the University of Bologna reported in an independent study that Alice has helped auditors stop irregular tenders across Brazil. She did not examine these tenders. ALICE (Analisador de Licitações, Contratos e Editais) is the in-house tool of the Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU). It reads procurement documents with artificial-intelligence techniques. It issues alerts about risk. The national procurement portal shows that tender 90017/2024 was published on 14 August 2024. On 14 January 2025 the CGU reported that ALICE had marked three 2024 tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state. At the Hospital Federal de Ipanema, tender 90016/2024 for laminated gowns (estimated R$16,726,635.12) was suspended after auditors confirmed an overpricing risk of R$10,925,029.92. Tender 90017/2024 for nursing supplies (estimated R$15,450,714.80) had an overpricing risk of R$5,994,645.60. It was re-estimated at R$12,386,939.96, a saving of R$3,063,774.84. At the Hospital Federal dos Servidores do Estado, tender 90002/2024 (estimated R$26,578,591.02) was revoked after a confirmed risk of R$2,475,054.36. The CGU gives no total. The three confirmed risks sum to R$19,394,729.88. It gives no date for the suspension. It gives none for the revocation. The portal shows that the hospital bought surgical gloves under tender 90017/2024 in May 2025, after the re-estimate. No final prices are given, so the size of the saving at purchase is not known.
record.purpose: Brazil's federal comptroller built the tool to audit federal procurement notices continuously and detect risks, such as inflated price estimates, before contracts are awarded.

The result mattered to the two hospitals and to the federal budget. In one tender, the estimate fell by a documented R$3,063,774.84. A suspension and a revocation removed R$13.4 million of confirmed overpricing risk.
The effect is small at national scale. The three tenders were among 118,069 processes analyzed in 2024.

Developer and deployer are the same public body, so this is the body documenting its own tool. The CGU page is on record as an archived copy, because the live page was restricted during Brazil's 2026 electoral period.

data.retained_case_account: On 14 January 2025 the Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU) reported on ALICE (Analisador de Licitações, Contratos e Editais). ALICE, its in-house tool, reads procurement documents with artificial-intelligence techniques and issues risk alerts. It had flagged three 2024 tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state. At the Hospital Federal de Ipanema, tender 90016/2024 for laminated gowns (estimated R$16,726,635.12) was suspended after auditors confirmed an overpricing risk of R$10,925,029.92. Tender 90017/2024 for nursing supplies (estimated R$15,450,714.80) had an overpricing risk of R$5,994,645.60. It was re-estimated at R$12,386,939.96, a saving of R$3,063,774.84. At the Hospital Federal dos Servidores do Estado, tender 90002/2024 (estimated R$26,578,591.02) was revoked after a confirmed risk of R$2,475,054.36. The release gives no total. The three confirmed risks sum to R$19,394,729.88, the R$19.4 million of the headline and metric. The release gives no dates for the suspension and revocation.

fields.account: In March 2023 Fernanda Odilla of the University of Bologna reported in an independent study that Alice has helped auditors stop irregular tenders across Brazil. She did not examine these tenders. ALICE (Analisador de Licitações, Contratos e Editais) is the in-house tool of the Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU). It reads procurement documents with artificial-intelligence techniques. It issues alerts about risk. The national procurement portal shows that tender 90017/2024 was published on 14 August 2024. On 14 January 2025 the CGU reported that ALICE had marked three 2024 tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state. At the Hospital Federal de Ipanema, tender 90016/2024 for laminated gowns (estimated R$16,726,635.12) was suspended after auditors confirmed an overpricing risk of R$10,925,029.92. Tender 90017/2024 for nursing supplies (estimated R$15,450,714.80) had an overpricing risk of R$5,994,645.60. It was re-estimated at R$12,386,939.96, a saving of R$3,063,774.84. At the Hospital Federal dos Servidores do Estado, tender 90002/2024 (estimated R$26,578,591.02) was revoked after a confirmed risk of R$2,475,054.36. The CGU gives no total. The three confirmed risks sum to R$19,394,729.88. It gives no date for the suspension. It gives none for the revocation. The portal shows that the hospital bought surgical gloves under tender 90017/2024 in May 2025, after the re-estimate. No final prices are given, so the size of the saving at purchase is not known.

display.answer: The archived CGU release of 14 January 2025 is the auditor's own account of the three tenders. The news reports of 21 and 28 January 2025 restate the release, and the first of them states that it draws on information from the CGU. Fernanda Odilla's independent study of March 2023 covers Alice across Brazil and does not examine these tenders. The procurement portal record of 23 May 2025 comes from the hospital and shows only that tender 90017/2024 went on to a purchase.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: ALICE, a tool of the CGU, flagged three 2024 tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state. Auditors confirmed R$19.4m of overpricing risk. Two tenders were stopped. The third was re-estimated.
fields.account: In March 2023 Fernanda Odilla of the University of Bologna reported in an independent study that Alice has helped auditors stop irregular tenders across Brazil. She did not examine these tenders. ALICE (Analisador de Licitações, Contratos e Editais) is the in-house tool of the Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU). It reads procurement documents with artificial-intelligence techniques. It issues alerts about risk. The national procurement portal shows that tender 90017/2024 was published on 14 August 2024. On 14 January 2025 the CGU reported that ALICE had marked three 2024 tenders of federal hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state. At the Hospital Federal de Ipanema, tender 90016/2024 for laminated gowns (estimated R$16,726,635.12) was suspended after auditors confirmed an overpricing risk of R$10,925,029.92. Tender 90017/2024 for nursing supplies (estimated R$15,450,714.80) had an overpricing risk of R$5,994,645.60. It was re-estimated at R$12,386,939.96, a saving of R$3,063,774.84. At the Hospital Federal dos Servidores do Estado, tender 90002/2024 (estimated R$26,578,591.02) was revoked after a confirmed risk of R$2,475,054.36. The CGU gives no total. The three confirmed risks sum to R$19,394,729.88. It gives no date for the suspension. It gives none for the revocation. The portal shows that the hospital bought surgical gloves under tender 90017/2024 in May 2025, after the re-estimate. No final prices are given, so the size of the saving at purchase is not known.

record.title: Metropolitan Police live facial recognition flags a sex offender at Denmark Hill who is alone with a six-year-old girl in breach of his court order
record.summary: The Metropolitan Police's Live Facial Recognition cameras identified a sex offender who was alone with a six-year-old girl on 10 January 2025. He was jailed for two years.
record.account: In January 2025 Metropolitan Police Live Facial Recognition cameras on a van at Denmark Hill identified a 73-year-old man. BBC News reports that officers stopped him on 10 January 2025. He was under a 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order that barred him from being alone with children under 14. The order followed a 2010 conviction for 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16. The conviction included five counts of gross indecency with a child. Officers found him with a six-year-old girl that he had collected from school for her mother. The mother did not know his history. A lock knife was hidden in his belt buckle. He pleaded guilty at Wimbledon Magistrates' Court on 13 January 2025 to breaching the order. His guilty pleas included one to possessing an offensive weapon. On 20 May 2025 Kingston Crown Court jailed him for two years. On 4 July 2025 the Met announced more than 1,000 arrests through live facial recognition. It published the man's story as one of its examples. On 21 April 2026 the High Court dismissed a challenge to the Met's policy on live facial recognition. It held that the policy is lawful, including its watchlists of offenders under court orders. The judges said that they had not been asked to consider whether the technology is effective. The claimants were Silkie Carlo of Big Brother Watch and Shaun Thompson, who had been misidentified by the system at London Bridge. In May 2026 William Page of Birmingham Law School wrote that Thompson intends to appeal.
record.purpose: The Met deploys Live Facial Recognition cameras on police vans to identify people of interest and alert officers. Its LFR lead, Lindsey Chiswick, describes the aim as using data and technology to identify offenders that pose a risk to our communities.
record.system: Live Facial Recognition (LFR) cameras mounted on a Metropolitan Police van
record.deployer: Metropolitan Police Service
record.segment: Law enforcement use of live facial recognition in public places

ratings.reason: A six-year-old girl was taken out of unsupervised contact with a man convicted of 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16. He had collected her from school for her mother and was carrying a lock knife. The Met's officer said only that abuse was possible, and no allegation about this occasion is reported.

A registered sex offender in breach of his order was jailed for two years. The Met presents this as removing a dangerous offender from the streets. On 21 April 2026 the High Court held that the Met's policy is lawful, and the judges said that they had not considered whether the technology is effective. The wider benefit is therefore contested.

Officers found the child and the knife, and the arrest, the charges and the sentence were the work of police and courts. The offense itself existed only because of his 2019 order. What would otherwise have happened is the Met's own hedge. DC Adam Pearce said that it is possible that, had he not been identified, the man could have gone on to abuse the child. No allegation about this occasion is reported. The vendor and the algorithm are not named in this benefit's sources.

produced_by: A van-mounted LFR deployment at Denmark Hill in January 2025 and a face the system was able to identify. The match alerted officers on the spot.
Officers who stopped him at once and found the child and the lock knife hidden in his belt buckle. They knew the terms of his 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order.
A court record of the order and his 2010 convictions. This turned the stop into a guilty plea for breaching the order and possessing an offensive weapon.
must_hold: The person must be known to the system and subject to conditions that make his presence with a child an offense. The benefit depends on the prior order, not on the camera alone.
Officers must verify the match and intervene immediately. The child was found only because he was stopped on the spot.
The deployment must be lawful and proportionate. The protective benefit therefore sits beside a contested surveillance practice.

data.retained_case_account: In January 2025 Metropolitan Police Live Facial Recognition (LFR) cameras on a van at Denmark Hill identified a 73-year-old man. He was under a 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order barring him from being alone with children under 14. The order followed a 2010 conviction for 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16 and five of gross indecency with a child. Officers found him with a six-year-old girl he had collected from school for her mother. The mother did not know his history. A lock knife was hidden in his belt buckle. He pleaded guilty at Wimbledon Magistrates' Court on 13 January 2025 to breaching the order and possessing an offensive weapon. On 20 May 2025 Kingston Crown Court jailed him for two years.

fields.account: In January 2025 Metropolitan Police Live Facial Recognition cameras on a van at Denmark Hill identified a 73-year-old man. BBC News reports that officers stopped him on 10 January 2025. He was under a 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order that barred him from being alone with children under 14. The order followed a 2010 conviction for 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16. The conviction included five counts of gross indecency with a child. Officers found him with a six-year-old girl that he had collected from school for her mother. The mother did not know his history. A lock knife was hidden in his belt buckle. He pleaded guilty at Wimbledon Magistrates' Court on 13 January 2025 to breaching the order. His guilty pleas included one to possessing an offensive weapon. On 20 May 2025 Kingston Crown Court jailed him for two years. On 4 July 2025 the Met announced more than 1,000 arrests through live facial recognition. It published the man's story as one of its examples. On 21 April 2026 the High Court dismissed a challenge to the Met's policy on live facial recognition. It held that the policy is lawful, including its watchlists of offenders under court orders. The judges said that they had not been asked to consider whether the technology is effective. The claimants were Silkie Carlo of Big Brother Watch and Shaun Thompson, who had been misidentified by the system at London Bridge. In May 2026 William Page of Birmingham Law School wrote that Thompson intends to appeal.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: Screenshots attached to the post show Grok answering three questions about the uploaded image. It said that there is “a clear fracture line visible in the distal radius”. record.summary: A mother posted on 11 January 2025 that Grok on X had flagged a displaced wrist fracture that urgent care missed. An orthopedist confirmed the fracture before putting the wrist in a cast.
record.account: On 11 January 2025 AJ Kay (@AJKayWriter, United States) posted about a multi-vehicle freeway crash the weekend before. An urgent-care doctor had read her teenage daughter's wrist X-rays as free of breaks. A radiologist read them the same way. They sent her home with an ace wrap. They gave her ibuprofen. Her daughter's hand was cold. It tingled. The thumb would not move. Kay uploaded the printed X-ray to Grok on X. It said that there was “a clear fracture line in the distal radius” and called it “quite obvious”. According to Grok, the line was “a fracture line rather than a fused growth plate”. After a referral from a primary-care physician, a wrist specialist took new X-rays the next day. The specialist diagnosed a distal radial head fracture with dorsal displacement. The arm was cast. The specialist said that untreated displacement would likely have needed surgery. Later on 11 January 2025 Elon Musk posted that “Grok can diagnose medical injuries”. The next day Grok told a physician who asked that it cannot diagnose medical injuries. In 2026 two independent studies tested later versions of Grok on fracture images. Hand surgeons led from Magdeburg found that Grok 4.1 detected 39.6% of 50 known distal radius fractures. They found that it judged displacement correctly in 34.8%. A Mayo Clinic team found that Grok 3 correctly diagnosed 18.8% of fracture images of the ankle, knee, hip and arm.
record.purpose: xAI built Grok as a general chatbot on X that accepts images. On 3 January 2025 Elon Musk invited users to upload “any image to Grok for analysis, from medical tests to video games”. So reading an X-ray was a use that Musk promoted, though xAI did not design Grok for clinical work. Grok's own replies told the user to consult a professional. When a physician asked it the next day, it said that it cannot diagnose medical injuries.

It said that there was “a clear fracture line in the distal radius” and called it “quite obvious”. According to Grok, the line was “a fracture line rather than a fused growth plate”. After a referral from a primary-care physician, a wrist specialist took new X-rays the next day. The specialist diagnosed a distal radial head fracture with dorsal displacement. The arm was cast. The specialist said that untreated displacement would likely have needed surgery. Later on 11 January 2025 Elon Musk posted that “Grok can diagnose medical injuries”. The next day Grok told a physician who asked that it cannot diagnose medical injuries. In 2026 two independent studies tested later versions of Grok on fracture images. Hand surgeons led from Magdeburg found that Grok 4.1 detected 39.6% of 50 known distal radius fractures. They found that it judged displacement correctly in 34.8%. A Mayo Clinic team found that Grok 3 correctly diagnosed 18.8% of fracture images of the ankle, knee, hip and arm.

record.title: Paraná's Court of Justice upheld IBAMA action against Atlantic Forest clearing flagged by MapBiomas Alerta in a 2021 decision, then again in 2024
record.summary: Paraná's Court of Justice kept a regeneration injunction in 2021 and upheld a repair order in 2024 for clearings of 49.41 ha and 17.40 ha that IBAMA pursued with MapBiomas alerts.
record.account: MapBiomas compiles deforestation alerts. It has analysts validate them on Planet images. It refines each outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. IBAMA, Brazil's federal environmental agency, used such alerts against Atlantic Forest clearing in southern Paraná. In its 2019 report on one clearing, IBAMA cites a MapBiomas alert that put the area at 40.86 ha. Agents walked the edge with GPS. They measured 49.41 ha. The report described the alert as experimental. On 10 May 2021 the Court of Justice of Paraná kept an injunction that requires the defendants to let the 49.41 ha regrow. State prosecutors had sought it. In 2021 IBAMA staff combined multitemporal satellite analysis with a MapBiomas alert. They issued a notice for destroying 17.40 ha. On 16 December 2024 the court upheld an order to repair that area. It found no defect in the notice. The landowner had not defended the case at first instance. In both decisions the court left the alerts unexamined. It did not reject the satellite evidence in either decision.
record.purpose: MapBiomas built MapBiomas Alerta to compile, validate and refine deforestation alerts from detection systems across Brazil and to publish each confirmed clearing with a report.
record.system: MapBiomas Alerta (the decisions call it 'alerta do MapBiomas', 'Alerta MapBiomas' or 'alerta do Mapbiomas')
record.developer: MapBiomas (MapBiomas Alerta), which compiles source alerts from other detection systems
record.deployer: IBAMA (Instituto Brasileiro do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Naturais Renováveis), Brazil's federal environmental agency, in southern Paraná. The Ministério Público do Paraná brought the civil actions.
record.location: Palmas and União da Vitória, Paraná, Brazil

fields.account: MapBiomas compiles deforestation alerts. It has analysts validate them on Planet images. It refines each outline with a supervised Random Forest classifier. IBAMA, Brazil's federal environmental agency, used such alerts against Atlantic Forest clearing in southern Paraná. In its 2019 report on one clearing, IBAMA cites a MapBiomas alert that put the area at 40.86 ha. Agents walked the edge with GPS. They measured 49.41 ha. The report described the alert as experimental. On 10 May 2021 the Court of Justice of Paraná kept an injunction that requires the defendants to let the 49.41 ha regrow. State prosecutors had sought it. In 2021 IBAMA staff combined multitemporal satellite analysis with a MapBiomas alert. They issued a notice for destroying 17.40 ha. On 16 December 2024 the court upheld an order to repair that area. It found no defect in the notice. The landowner had not defended the case at first instance. In both decisions the court left the alerts unexamined. It did not reject the satellite evidence in either decision.

record.title: GiveDirectly pays over 4,600 people in Kogi State, Nigeria, on Google Flood Hub forecasts, mostly before floods peaked in October 2024
record.summary: GiveDirectly used Google Flood Hub forecasts to trigger $105 payments to over 4,600 people in Ibaji, Kogi State, most of them before floods peaked on 21 October 2024.
record.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts through an application programming interface. It made maps of inundation. It set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored the forecasts daily. It cross-checked them with observations from communities. The trigger was met when forecasts showed that 20% of a community's area would flood. Verified residents were then paid. The New Humanitarian later described an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports that it sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. It paid 3,250 people between 29 August and 6 October 2024. It paid 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. On 14 October 2025 Rest of World reported that GiveDirectly planned a 2026 randomized trial of the approach in northern Bangladesh, covering over 100,000 families. Rest of World gave 4,463 as the number of people paid early in Kogi, a lower figure than GiveDirectly's count of over 4,600. GiveDirectly updated its page in July 2026, according to a note on it. On 31 August 2026 The New Humanitarian published an investigation. Its reporters found that mismatches in the data excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. They found that barriers to phone access did the same. GiveDirectly told the outlet that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably.
record.purpose: GiveDirectly used the forecasts to decide when and where to send cash, so that it reached flood-prone communities before the river flooded.

ratings.reason: GiveDirectly sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals, and a $210 transfer followed. How many people received the second transfer is not known. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports that weekly income more than doubled and that food shortages fell. The sources show no independent check of these survey figures.

GiveDirectly gained a tested trigger pipeline and documented lessons. It acknowledged to The New Humanitarian that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. GiveDirectly updated its page in July 2026, according to a note there, before the investigation was published on 31 August 2026.

The cash that reached about 4,600 people is the personal benefit already rated, and GiveDirectly has reported no measured change for the 53 communities as a whole. The New Humanitarian also documents that some of the poorest residents were excluded.

data.retained_case_account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.

fields.summary: GiveDirectly used Google Flood Hub forecasts to trigger $105 payments to over 4,600 people in Ibaji, Kogi State, most of them before floods peaked on 21 October 2024.
fields.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts through an application programming interface. It made maps of inundation. It set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored the forecasts daily. It cross-checked them with observations from communities. The trigger was met when forecasts showed that 20% of a community's area would flood. Verified residents were then paid. The New Humanitarian later described an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports that it sent $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. It paid 3,250 people between 29 August and 6 October 2024. It paid 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. In its own survey, GiveDirectly reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. On 14 October 2025 Rest of World reported that GiveDirectly planned a 2026 randomized trial of the approach in northern Bangladesh, covering over 100,000 families. Rest of World gave 4,463 as the number of people paid early in Kogi, a lower figure than GiveDirectly's count of over 4,600. GiveDirectly updated its page in July 2026, according to a note on it. On 31 August 2026 The New Humanitarian published an investigation. Its reporters found that mismatches in the data excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. They found that barriers to phone access did the same. GiveDirectly told the outlet that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably.

record.title: Crews hold the Wellington fire near Breckenridge to one-eighth acre after a Pano AI camera funded by Xcel Energy spots it
record.summary: A Pano AI camera funded by Xcel Energy alerted crews to a campsite fire near a Breckenridge neighborhood. Firefighters said that the early notice kept it to one-eighth of an acre.
record.account: The Wellington fire broke out on Sunday, 7 July 2024, at an unattended campsite just east of a Breckenridge neighborhood. Summit Daily reported on 8 July 2024 that crews were dispatched around 12:30 p.m. The officials whom it interviewed credited fuels reduction work completed 18 months earlier for the containment within hours. They did not mention the camera. Summit Daily gave the fire's size as up to a quarter-acre. CBS Colorado reported on 9 July 2024 that the fire was spotted by a Pano AI camera financially supported by Xcel Energy. The camera sits on a cell tower with a 360-degree view. It sends an alert to emergency crews when it detects smoke. Firefighters said that this was the first instance in Summit County where a wildfire was caught early thanks to the camera. They said that the early notice kept it to one-eighth of an acre. Earlier alerts had been false alarms from legal campfires. Mathew Benedict of Red White and Blue Fire's Wildland Division said that a location given as latitude and longitude let crews drive straight to the fire. Otherwise they could spend up to an hour finding it. Michelle Aguayo of Xcel Energy said that the company had 28 Pano AI cameras installed. On 3 September 2024 CBS Colorado reported that Pano AI cameras had first spotted another one-eighth-acre fire near the Gold Hill Trailhead. KJCT8 reported on 5 May 2026 that Xcel Energy had more than 130 Pano AI cameras across Colorado.

They said that the early notice kept it to one-eighth of an acre. Earlier alerts had been false alarms from legal campfires. Mathew Benedict of Red White and Blue Fire's Wildland Division said that a location given as latitude and longitude let crews drive straight to the fire. Otherwise they could spend up to an hour finding it. Michelle Aguayo of Xcel Energy said that the company had 28 Pano AI cameras installed. On 3 September 2024 CBS Colorado reported that Pano AI cameras had first spotted another one-eighth-acre fire near the Gold Hill Trailhead. KJCT8 reported on 5 May 2026 that Xcel Energy had more than 130 Pano AI cameras across Colorado.

record.title: Cal Fire sends engines to a fire near Auburn that ALERTCalifornia cameras flag before any 911 call
record.summary: Software from DigitalPath on ALERTCalifornia cameras spotted smoke near Auburn at 2:33 a.m. on 6 July 2024, before any 911 call. Crews kept the fire to a 30 x 30 foot area.
record.account: The University of California San Diego runs the ALERTCalifornia network of cameras. The network uses software that detects smoke. The software comes from DigitalPath of Chico, California. Cal Fire uses the network. At 2:33 a.m. on 6 July the network posted an alert about a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The reporter wrote in September 2025. The story gave the day of the fire. It left out the year. The fire appears among the previous year's fires in that story, so this benefit is dated 2024. In the reporter's account, no 911 call had come in. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center checked the alert. Then it sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said that in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. The cameras detected 636 of those fires before anyone called 911. By October 2026 the network had grown to nearly 1,300 cameras. The program director planned 1,800.
record.purpose: The software looks for smoke in the images from the cameras and alerts the dispatchers of fire services on its own. It did so near Auburn.

data.retained_case_account: The ALERTCalifornia camera network is operated by UC San Diego with AI smoke-detection software from DigitalPath of Chico, California, and used by Cal Fire. It posted an alert at 2:33 a.m. on July 6 of a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The report, from September 2025, gives the day but not the year. It places the case among the previous year's fires, so 2024 is used. Nobody had called 911. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center verified the alert and sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. Of those, 636 came before any person called 911.

record.title: Pano AI cameras on Xcel and CORE Electric towers spot the Bear Creek Fire, which is held to three acres
record.summary: Pano AI cameras detected smoke from the Bear Creek Fire in Douglas County, Colorado, on 16 June 2024. Helicopters were sent within 30 minutes, and the fire was held to three acres.
record.account: On 16 June 2024, at about 9:30 a.m., Pano AI cameras that watch for wildfires detected smoke. They stood on towers of Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. In their original joint statement, the utilities say that the cameras and the U.S. Forest Service spotted the smoke at the same time. They say that helicopters launched at 9:54 a.m. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The utilities specify 5.5 hours of helicopter operations. They specify 17,765 gallons of water. By 7 p.m., they report, the fire was contained at three acres. In the statement, Mike Alexander of the Douglas County Sheriff's Office says that the situation could have grown much worse by noon without the early data. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day. It reported that the AI-equipped cameras first spotted it. In that report, CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said that alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. Because the utilities report that the Forest Service detected the fire at the same time, the cameras' own contribution to containment rests on the operators' statements. Among them are those of CORE's interim CEO, Pam Feuerstein. CBS Colorado reported in May 2025 that Pano had 86 camera stations in Colorado, with 163 planned.
record.purpose: Pano AI built its cameras to rotate 360 degrees on mountaintop towers and detect plumes of smoke with AI. They alert utilities and fire agencies with a triangulated location.
record.system: Pano AI wildfire detection cameras (Pano Rapid Detect)
record.deployer: Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative

ratings.reason: The fire was held to three acres after helicopters were dispatched within 30 minutes. CORE's CEO called the detection and location “crucial”. The Forest Service spotted the fire at the same time, which limits what can be credited to the cameras.

Xcel Energy and CORE Electric have not reported an outcome of their own, such as damage avoided to their lines or equipment. The alert served the response of the county and the Forest Service. The claim that alerts typically beat 911 calls is about the system in general.
No individual who benefited is documented.

ai_role.statement: The AI's detection of smoke supplied an alert and a location. In their original joint account, CORE and Xcel state that the cameras identified the fire at the same time as the U.S. Forest Service. They describe how the coordinates helped the response, but they do not establish what the AI added to the outcome of three acres.

data.retained_case_account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The original joint utility statement specifies 5.5 hours of helicopter operations, 17,765 gallons of water, and containment at three acres by 7 p.m. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein).

fields.account: On 16 June 2024, at about 9:30 a.m., Pano AI cameras that watch for wildfires detected smoke. They stood on towers of Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. In their original joint statement, the utilities say that the cameras and the U.S. Forest Service spotted the smoke at the same time. They say that helicopters launched at 9:54 a.m. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The utilities specify 5.5 hours of helicopter operations. They specify 17,765 gallons of water. By 7 p.m., they report, the fire was contained at three acres. In the statement, Mike Alexander of the Douglas County Sheriff's Office says that the situation could have grown much worse by noon without the early data. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day. It reported that the AI-equipped cameras first spotted it. In that report, CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said that alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. Because the utilities report that the Forest Service detected the fire at the same time, the cameras' own contribution to containment rests on the operators' statements. Among them are those of CORE's interim CEO, Pam Feuerstein. CBS Colorado reported in May 2025 that Pano had 86 camera stations in Colorado, with 163 planned.

record.title: Transport for West Midlands: detecting near misses with VivaCity
record.summary: Transport for West Midlands reports that VivaCity sensors detected 61,000 near misses. At one Coventry junction, near misses fell by more than 88 percent after a refuge was built.
record.account: Transport for West Midlands enabled VivaCity near-miss detection in 40 sensors. It used the observations to select road-layout changes. It then implemented them. It reports 61,000 detected near misses in six months. The measures that it reports installing include central islands. Junction mouths were narrowed. It documents the measures. It reports no reduction in collisions or injuries. On 5 February 2025 Coventry City Council was still set to install a pedestrian refuge at Grange Road after the sensors recorded near misses there. On 18 November 2025 TfWM reported that near misses at the junction fell by more than 88 percent after the refuge was built. TfWM gave no data on collisions or injuries.

fields.summary: Transport for West Midlands reports that VivaCity sensors detected 61,000 near misses. At one Coventry junction, near misses fell by more than 88 percent after a refuge was built.
fields.account: Transport for West Midlands enabled VivaCity near-miss detection in 40 sensors. It used the observations to select road-layout changes. It then implemented them. It reports 61,000 detected near misses in six months. The measures that it reports installing include central islands. Junction mouths were narrowed. It documents the measures. It reports no reduction in collisions or injuries. On 5 February 2025 Coventry City Council was still set to install a pedestrian refuge at Grange Road after the sensors recorded near misses there. On 18 November 2025 TfWM reported that near misses at the junction fell by more than 88 percent after the refuge was built. TfWM gave no data on collisions or injuries.

record.title: A ZeroEyes detection in the parking lot of Hobbs' Del Norte Pool leads police to clay shooters near a street, one of whom is charged
record.summary: ZeroEyes reports that on 30 November 2023 its gun detection alerted Hobbs police to a gun on a camera in the Del Norte Pool parking lot. Officers detained people shooting clays.
record.account: The Odessa American (reproduced by GovTech) reports, from a ZeroEyes news release, on an alert at 6:35 p.m. MDT on 30 November 2023. ZeroEyes alerted the Hobbs Police Department and the Eagle I.C. dispatch center. A gun had been detected on a security camera in Del Norte Pool's parking lot. Those involved were shooting sporting clays close to North Grimes Street. Responding officers detained them. Then charges were filed against one. Hobbs Police Chief August Fons is quoted as saying that detection and rapid human verification helped stop the activity before anyone was hurt. He said that in the past something like this would have been missed entirely. Lubbock Lights later reported ZeroEyes co-founder Sam Alaimo showing images from the incident. He said that it resulted in an arrest with no one hurt. He listed the City of Hobbs and its school system among local clients. Lubbock Lights describes the images from the Del Norte Pool lot that the co-founder showed as a person pointing a gun in the general direction of a distant vehicle. In its release, ZeroEyes describes people shooting sporting clays near North Grimes Street. No court record has been found.

fields.account: The Odessa American (reproduced by GovTech) reports, from a ZeroEyes news release, on an alert at 6:35 p.m. MDT on 30 November 2023. ZeroEyes alerted the Hobbs Police Department and the Eagle I.C. dispatch center. A gun had been detected on a security camera in Del Norte Pool's parking lot. Those involved were shooting sporting clays close to North Grimes Street. Responding officers detained them. Then charges were filed against one. Hobbs Police Chief August Fons is quoted as saying that detection and rapid human verification helped stop the activity before anyone was hurt. He said that in the past something like this would have been missed entirely. Lubbock Lights later reported ZeroEyes co-founder Sam Alaimo showing images from the incident. He said that it resulted in an arrest with no one hurt. He listed the City of Hobbs and its school system among local clients. Lubbock Lights describes the images from the Del Norte Pool lot that the co-founder showed as a person pointing a gun in the general direction of a distant vehicle. In its release, ZeroEyes describes people shooting sporting clays near North Grimes Street. No court record has been found.

record.title: LAPD sends its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped onto a Hollywood Metro bus during a two-hour standoff with a sleeping man whose gun proves to be a BB gun
record.summary: A Los Angeles police drone observed a sleeping man with a suspected gun on a bus. Officers then sent in the Boston Dynamics Spot robot as a barrier. The gun proved to be a BB gun.
record.account: Just before 4 a.m. on 8 November 2023, a passenger on a Metro bus in Hollywood reported an armed man aboard. The bus was at Melrose and Western avenues. The driver pulled over. He evacuated the other passengers. Officers got no response from the man. A two-hour standoff followed (Los Angeles Times via Police1, 9 November 2023). In its quarterly report, the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) says that patrol officers tried to talk with the man for about 75 minutes. They then declared an armed barricade. They called the special weapons and tactics (SWAT) team. The LAPD sent in its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. The LAPD states that a drone observed the sleeping man before the quadruped entered. It states that the drone also observed the suspected gun. It adds that SWAT chose the quadruped because a tracked robot could not have climbed the bus steps. By the LAPD's account, the quadruped climbed the bus steps. It then formed a barrier between the man and the suspected firearm. The LAPD does not describe the robot removing the weapon. The man woke. He left the bus. He was taken into custody about 6:40 a.m. The weapon was a BB gun (Police1). Police1 attributes the initial observation to the quadruped’s camera. In an account of October 2024, International Business Times says that the robot removed the gun. Deputy Chief David Kowalski approves each use. The robot cost nearly $300,000 (NBC). By 1 January 2025 SWAT had deployed the robot at least seven times, Spectrum News reported.
record.purpose: Boston Dynamics built Spot. The department acquired it, in Deputy Chief Kowalski's words, “to save lives” by putting a camera and an articulating arm into dangerous scenes ahead of officers.

fields.summary: A Los Angeles police drone observed a sleeping man with a suspected gun on a bus. Officers then sent in the Boston Dynamics Spot robot as a barrier. The gun proved to be a BB gun.
fields.account: Just before 4 a.m. on 8 November 2023, a passenger on a Metro bus in Hollywood reported an armed man aboard. The bus was at Melrose and Western avenues. The driver pulled over. He evacuated the other passengers. Officers got no response from the man. A two-hour standoff followed (Los Angeles Times via Police1, 9 November 2023). In its quarterly report, the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) says that patrol officers tried to talk with the man for about 75 minutes. They then declared an armed barricade. They called the special weapons and tactics (SWAT) team. The LAPD sent in its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. The LAPD states that a drone observed the sleeping man before the quadruped entered. It states that the drone also observed the suspected gun. It adds that SWAT chose the quadruped because a tracked robot could not have climbed the bus steps. By the LAPD's account, the quadruped climbed the bus steps. It then formed a barrier between the man and the suspected firearm. The LAPD does not describe the robot removing the weapon. The man woke. He left the bus. He was taken into custody about 6:40 a.m. The weapon was a BB gun (Police1). Police1 attributes the initial observation to the quadruped’s camera. In an account of October 2024, International Business Times says that the robot removed the gun. Deputy Chief David Kowalski approves each use. The robot cost nearly $300,000 (NBC). By 1 January 2025 SWAT had deployed the robot at least seven times, Spectrum News reported.

record.title: After a model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection flags a car at San Ysidro, officers arrest two people with over 75 kg of narcotics (2023)
record.summary: A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection flagged a car's crossing history at San Ysidro in 2023. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics. They arrested two people.
record.account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Port of Entry at San Ysidro. A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection detected a suspicious pattern in its crossing history. The model marked the car for review. The alert came in under 1.4 seconds. An officer referred the car to secondary inspection. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics in the rear quarter panels. More was in the gas tank. They seized the drugs. They seized the vehicle. They arrested the driver. They arrested the passenger. Eric Hysen, chief information officer of the Department of Homeland Security, described the event in congressional testimony on 14 September 2023. In his testimony he says that the car crossed recently. He gives no date. He said that without the model an officer would have had no cause to inspect the car more closely than at a normal stop. He told Congress that referrals from these models had led to 240 seizures in 2023 by mid-September. On its page about artificial intelligence, last updated on 27 November 2023, the department describes the same seizure and the arrest of the driver. At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023, Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching event. He said that the model of the Office of Field Operations flagged in 1.4 seconds a “truck” that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. In its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap of March 2024, the department repeats the account as a referral for secondary review that yielded over 75 kilograms of drugs. The drug and the date of the seizure have not been reported.
record.purpose: According to the Department of Homeland Security's Artificial Intelligence Roadmap of 2024, U.S. Customs and Border Protection built the model to find possibly suspicious patterns in vehicles' crossing histories. It flags vehicles for secondary review at ports of entry.

fields.summary: A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection flagged a car's crossing history at San Ysidro in 2023. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics. They arrested two people.
fields.account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Port of Entry at San Ysidro. A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection detected a suspicious pattern in its crossing history. The model marked the car for review. The alert came in under 1.4 seconds. An officer referred the car to secondary inspection. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics in the rear quarter panels. More was in the gas tank. They seized the drugs. They seized the vehicle. They arrested the driver. They arrested the passenger. Eric Hysen, chief information officer of the Department of Homeland Security, described the event in congressional testimony on 14 September 2023. In his testimony he says that the car crossed recently. He gives no date. He said that without the model an officer would have had no cause to inspect the car more closely than at a normal stop. He told Congress that referrals from these models had led to 240 seizures in 2023 by mid-September. On its page about artificial intelligence, last updated on 27 November 2023, the department describes the same seizure and the arrest of the driver. At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023, Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching event. He said that the model of the Office of Field Operations flagged in 1.4 seconds a “truck” that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. In its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap of March 2024, the department repeats the account as a referral for secondary review that yielded over 75 kilograms of drugs. The drug and the date of the seizure have not been reported.

record.title: Cal Fire holds a fire near Mount Laguna to under a quarter acre after human operators verify smoke that ALERTCalifornia's AI flags at 3 am
record.summary: ALERTCalifornia's AI flagged smoke on a Cleveland National Forest camera at about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023. Cal Fire held the verified fire under a quarter acre.
record.account: The ALERTCalifornia AI, a machine-learned model run by the University of California San Diego, scans live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. It began scanning the feeds at the end of June 2023 in a trial with Cal Fire. At about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023, the AI picked out a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. Human operators verified the detection. They alerted Cal Fire. On 24 August 2023 the Los Angeles Times reported that Scott Slumpff, a battalion chief at Cal Fire, got the confirmed alert just before 3 a.m. The Times reported that crews held the fire to a spot 10 feet by 10 feet. Slumpff said that without the alert nobody would have known about the fire until the next morning. He judged that it would probably have reached hundreds of acres. On 12 September 2023 AFP reported that the operators had alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. It reported that his crews put the fire out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers. According to Cal Fire's figures for 2024, the cameras picked up 1,668 of 7,553 wildfires in its jurisdiction, 636 of them before any 911 call.
record.purpose: The University of California San Diego built the tool with Digital Path to spot smoke in the feeds of ALERTCalifornia's cameras and notify Cal Fire's emergency command centers. Crews can then reach a fire while it is starting.
record.system: ALERTCalifornia AI wildfire detection (machine-learned smoke and anomaly detection on the ALERTCalifornia pan-tilt-zoom camera network)

record.deployer: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE)

ratings.reason: Cal Fire's Mount Laguna station received a verified alert at about 3 a.m. Its crews put the fire out at under a quarter acre. Suzann Leininger, an intelligence specialist at Cal Fire, said: “It's getting us time to react in a faster manner”.

The area around Mount Laguna was spared a larger fire. Captain Yeary judged that it “could have been a devastating fire”. Battalion Chief Slumpff judged that it would probably have reached hundreds of acres. Neither judgment rests on a measurement of what would have happened without the alert.

The time gained is documented only for the program as a whole. TIME reports that 77 fires were identified before any 911 call in the first two months. Neal Driscoll of UC San Diego says that the alerts beat 911 calls about 40 percent of the time. AFP also notes false detections, which is why operators check each one before anyone is dispatched.

data.retained_case_account: At about 3 am on 5 August 2023, the ALERTCalifornia AI flagged a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. The AI, a machine-learned model run by UC San Diego, watches live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. Human operators verified the detection and alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. His crews put it out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. The AI watch over the feeds began at the end of June 2023 under a Cal Fire trial. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The model's contribution was the detection. Its algorithm flagged a smoke column in a Cleveland National Forest camera feed at about 3 am. Human operators verified it before Cal Fire was alerted. The containment was done by Captain Yeary's crews. No source records whether a 911 call would have come later. The time gained is documented only for the program as a whole. TIME reports 77 fires identified before any 911 call in the first two months. UC San Diego's Neal Driscoll says the alerts beat 911 calls about 40 percent of the time. AFP also notes the system sometimes misreads dust, insects or weather as smoke. That is why the human verification step sits between the model and the dispatch.
